metadata.title: Ways to buy or sell Super Bowl tickets without being defrauded
metadata.author: Arizona’s Family (3TV / CBS 5)
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re looking to buy or sell digital tickets to the Super Bowl, it’s best to avoid private parties advertising on the Internet.
  
#superbowl #football #azfamily #arizona #news #consumer #onyourside 
 For more Local News from KPHO:  https://www.azfamily.com/
 For more YouTube Content: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCIrgpHvUm1FMtv-C1xwkJtw

metadata.author: CBS Mornings
metadata.shortDescription: Super Bowl tickets can still be yours this morning, but the price is nothing short of astronomical. On StubHub, the world's largest source for second-hand tickets, they start at more than $7,000 dollars, with the top seats going for more than $40,000. Only on "CBS This Morning," Carter Evans reports on how far the company is going this weekend to protect buyers.

metadata.title: Cheapest Super Bowl Tickets for Last-Minute Buyers Are Running #tickets #scalping #superbowl
metadata.author: Yea Baby
metadata.shortDescription:
Guess How Much the Cheapest Super Bowl Tickets for Last-Minute Buyers Are Running
PHOENIX (TheBlaze/AP) — In previous years, the scenario for getting Super Bowl tickets at a reasonable price was simply waiting until the last possible minute to buy.

That was how it played out last year in New York where many fans got into MetLife Stadium by purchasing tickets the day of the game for less than the listed price.

But Sunday’s matchup between New England and Seattle is on pace to be the most expensive Super Bowl ticket in history. A shortage of tickets made available to brokers on the secondary market has driven prices into five figures even for nosebleed seats.
It’s left ticket companies having to offer refunds to buyers because the tickets never came through. And it’s left thousands of fans wandering around Phoenix without entry to University of Phoenix Stadium.

“I don’t have $10,000 that I want to give away,” Seahawks fan Mark Blair said.

As of midday Saturday the NFL Ticket Exchange, the league’s official ticket re-sale website, didn’t have tickets for less than $9,000. The cheapest ticket on StubHub was nearly the same. One listing on Craigslist in Phoenix was selling tickets for $8,000 each with the seller willing to meet the buyer at their bank to complete the transaction.

Cameron Papp, spokesman for StubHub, said the only other event that came close the level of ticket cost fans are seeing was the BCS championship game between Notre Dame and Alabama in Miami two years ago. Papp said the average ticket price sold on their site for this year’s game is currently $3,700. Last year it was $2,500.

“This is unprecedented really. We’ve never seen prices this high,” Papp said. “We have much lower inventory this year than we did in the past. A lot of people bought tickets early as compared to last year. Last year in New York everyone waited until the last couple of days to buy tickets because they were spooked by the weather. This year a lot of people bought early and we’re running out of tickets.”

The other factor is the higher demand because of the popularity of the two teams. Seattle fans have flooded the Phoenix area making the short 2 ½ hour flight from the Northwest.

Aside from chants of “Sea … Hawks!” the most popular phrase heard in downtown Phoenix late in the week was, “Anybody got extra tickets?”

Erik Olberg and his large group of friends from Seattle — numbering more than 30 — planned to follow the conventional pattern of getting tickets after arriving in Arizona. Olberg didn’t go to New York last year and heard the stories of how so many achieved success getting last-minute tickets at or below list price.

His group passed on buying tickets for $2,200 the day after the NFC championship game, convinced the prices would be lower. When they started to see the prices climbing earlier this week before leaving Seattle, checking websites became an hourly chore.

“I was checking every hour on StubHub, looking at where it’s going, trying to find an anomaly, just trying to get lucky,” Olberg said. “It’s just not happening. You hear of someone selling a ticket, but then you hear the price.”

In the case of Olberg and his friends, the concern now is trying to find somewhere to watch the game, but they’re going to explore every avenue to try and find a way in at a reasonable price.

“This is a once in a lifetime opportunity. We don’t know if the Seahawks are going to go back again,” Olberg said. “Who knows? I hope so but you don’t know that. I’m going to do everything I can until the last minute to try and go.”

metadata.title: How the VIP Super Bowl Experience Works with On Location President Paul Caine
metadata.author: Front Office Sports News
metadata.shortDescription:
From Super Bowl LX in San Francisco, Front Office Sports sits down with Paul Caine, President of On Location, the NFL’s official hospitality partner, to discuss the evolving business of live sports experiences.

At the Super Bowl, the game is only part of the business.

On Radio Row, On Location executive Paul Caine breaks down how the sports experience economy is reshaping the biggest events in the world—from the Super Bowl to the Olympics and World Cup.

We discuss:

• Why stadiums are being built as year-round destinations
• How premium hospitality and VIP access actually work
• The real dynamics behind Super Bowl ticket supply and pricing
• What the TKO (UFC + WWE) integration means for live events
• Why sports travel is becoming a trillion-dollar global market
• How the NFL continues to grow international demand

As fans increasingly spend on experiences instead of things, events like the Super Bowl remain the crown jewel of live sports.

Subscribe to Front Office Sports for interviews and insights at the intersection of sports, business, and culture.

0:00 Why the Super Bowl Experience Is Different in Every City
0:48 The Rise of Destination Stadiums & Entertainment Districts
1:40 Why Teams Need Real Estate Around Venues
2:30 How On Location Builds Super Bowl Experiences
3:20 What Changed After the TKO (UFC & WWE) Integration
4:20 The Growing Portfolio: NFL, Olympics, World Cup & More
5:05 Inside the Masters Partnership Conversation
5:55 How Super Bowl Ticket Supply & Pricing Actually Work
7:00 Why Demand Spikes After Teams Are Announced
8:10 What Fans Get With Premium Hospitality Access
9:00 Is the Super Bowl Still the #1 Bucket-List Sports Event?
10:00 The $600B Sports Travel Economy
11:05 Why Global Fans Are Driving NFL Growth

metadata.title: Inside the Super Bowl 2026 fan experience
metadata.author: FOX 13 Seattle
metadata.shortDescription:
Thousands of Seahawks fans who made the trip to the Bay Area were treated to an interactive Super Bowl Experience at San Francisco’s Moscone Center, where football exhibits, games, memorabilia and activities kicked off the celebration ahead of Sunday’s big game.

Watch FOX 13 Seattle Live: https://www.fox13seattle.com/live

FOX 13 Seattle is Western Washington's source for breaking news, weather, traffic, politics and sports.

Download the FOX LOCAL App: https://www.fox13seattle.com/apps

Download the FOX 13 Seattle Weather App: https://jckig.app.link/dlUcXuM2Peb

Subscribe to FOX 13 Seattle newsletters: https://www.fox13seattle.com/newsletters

Follow FOX 13 Seattle on TikTok: https://www.tiktok.com/@fox13seattle

metadata.title: StubHub officials discuss market for Super Bowl tickets, fan experience at amusement park
metadata.author: AP Archive
metadata.shortDescription:
(6 Feb 2016) SHOTLIST (including transcript):-
AP Entertainment
Santa Clara, 5 February 2016
1. Wide of Super Bowl tent adjacent to Levis Stadium
2. Tight of Super Bowl tent
3. Wide of carousel 
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Jason Deppen/StubHub, Director of Field Operations, on ticket prices for the Super Bowl:
"We're seeing prices as low as $3,000 dollars to get in, so we are talking upper corner, upper end zone. Those prices are hovering around 3,000. The average price we're seeing $4,500, $4,700, and prices get up to into the tens of thousands depending on suite levels, and lower sidelines of course."
5. Medium of carousel 
6. SOUNDBITE (English) Jason Deppen/StubHub, Director of Field Operations, on whether tickets will be left by kickoff on Sunday:
"We have not seen a lot of downward trend movement, which we have seen in the past at other Super Bowls. I don't know if I expect it to go too much down on how much inventory is left on game day."
7. Medium of painted horses on carousel
8. SOUNDBITE (English) Jason Deppen/StubHub, Director of Field Operations, on the teams playing sets ticket prices:
"It's true supply and demand. The market, which we like to see on StubHub, being open and transparent is that it always sets itself up for the match up."
9. Wide of roller coaster
10. Wide of Fan Fair signage on roller coaster
11. Medium of Justin Finn
12. SOUNDBITE (English) Justin Finn/StubHub, Head of Event Marketing, on renting out amusement park for Super Bowl weekend:
"We've acquired Great American Theme Park. We've got three roller coasters, six additional park rides, and five park games, plus athletes throughout the day, meet and greets. We've got a live radio broadcast on a national sports radio network. We'll have face painters, carnival type games, plus free hospitality throughout the day."
13. Wide of carousel 
14. Fan Fair signage
15. SOUNDBITE (English) Justin Finn/StubHub, Head of Event Marketing, on the event:
"This is actually a free experience for any StubHub customer, so if you buy your ticket on StubHub for the Super Bowl, this is a gif to you back from us. It's a little surprise and delight, and something we like to do for all of our fans. This is the eight year in a row that we have done a Super Bowl experience for free for our customers."
16. Wide of Great America 
STUBHUB OFFICIALS ON LATEST SUPER BOWL TICKET PRICES, FAN FARE
For a mere $3,000 dollars (USD) you can attend the Super Bowl.
That's the bottom price of a ticket to the big game Sunday, according to an official from the online ticket broker, StubHub.
Director of field operations, Jason Deppen says prices are holding steady.
"We're seeing prices as low as $3,000 dollars to get in, so we are talking upper corner, upper end zone. Those prices are hovering around 3,000. The average price we're seeing $4,500, $4,700, and prices get up to into the tens of thousands depending on suite levels, and lower sidelines of course," he said.
Deppen says StubHub has already sold nearly 5,000 tickets, and expects sales to reach 6,000 before kickoff.
"We have not seen a lot of downward trend movement, which we have seen in the past at other Super Bowls. I don't know if I expect it to go too much down on how much inventory is left on game day," he said.
According to Deppen, simply supply and demand, as well as the teams that make it, dictates the ticket price.
"The market, which we like to see on StubHub, being open and transparent is that it always sets itself up for the match up," Deppen noted.
Justin Finn, Head of Event Marketing explains.
The amusement park is adjacent to the stadium.

metadata.title: How much? Browns fans outraged by possible personal seat-license (PSL) pricing in Brook Park.
metadata.author: News 5 Cleveland
metadata.shortDescription: As the Browns cobble together financing for a $2.4 billion enclosed stadium in Brook Park, PSLs could be a key piece of the puzzle. Money from season ticket holders would help cover the team’s costs. A recent Browns survey showed PSLs could cost anywhere from $550 to $193,650 a seat. The median price for a PSL was $4,475. The team says it’s getting feedback from fans – and hasn’t made any decisions.

metadata.shortDescription:
Click here to subscribe: https://bit.ly/2Rad2N8

00:00 \\ Introduction
00:34 \\ 1 - Selling Locally
1:45 \\ 2 - Building Your Client List
3:43 \\ 3 - Listing Tickets Early
5:37 \\ 4 - Playoffs Playoffs Playoffs
6:36 \\ Potential Profit Examples
8:17 \\ Conclusion

Want to learn how to make money buying and selling season tickets? All that info and more is inside! I even share how much I made selling my season tickets during the Toronto Raptors 2019 championship run to the NBA Finals!

1) Sell locally. If you can find ticket buyers in your local area, then you'll be at an advantage to everyone selling tickets online. You can directly communicate with ticket buyers, negotiate prices, and still come out ahead compared to those who are selling their tickets online and dealing with large transaction fees and commissions. 

2) Build a client list. Like the above, as you sell tickets locally, you'll also start to develop client relationships. Use this to your advantage so that you can contact them again in the future. As you build up your list of clients, this will become more valuable down the road since you'll be able to rely on them to purchase tickets from you each and every season, along with those magical playoff runs. 

3) Ability to list tickets early. This is a big one, especially if you are not able to sell locally. Once a new season and schedule is announced, you'll be able to list your tickets early and potentially make outsized returns on early sales since there will be much less competition for available tickets. Things will eventually normalize, but at the onset you'll be one of the few with listings available for purchase and could potentially make a lot of money selling those season tickets early on.

4) Playoffs playoffs playoffs. This is the golden goose of owning season tickets. When a team qualifies for the playoffs, this is where all your patience and dedication to the team pay off. You can earn large returns well in excess of the regular season profits should your team both qualify for the playoffs and potentially head all the way to the championship round/games in their respective leagues. The 2019 Toronto Raptors run led me to earn huge profits which are shared in this video.

Sign up for Rakuten and start earning cash-back on every single ticket purchase: https://bit.ly/37b8vji

metadata.title: How seat licenses work

metadata.shortDescription: MPR's Tim Nelson explains how the seat licenses at the new Vikings stadium will work.

segments.text: I'm Tim Nelson from Minnesota Public
Radio one of the most controversial
aspects of the new Vikings stadium is a
change that will be happening in the
stands and in fans wallets it's personal
seat licensing here in Minnesota
lawmakers called them stadium builder
licenses seat licenses are one way NFL
teams pay for expensive new stadiums
about half the league's teams have them
here's how they work at the Metrodome
buying a ticket for a Vikings game is a
little like renting an apartment you
have a given location for a given period
of time after the game or the season you
and your seat part ways you might extend
your lease or not if you give up your
seat or your season tickets someone else
will move in now think of the new
stadium as more of a condominium
development like a condo the stadium is
being subdivided into pieces that are up
for sale and Vikings fans will be buying
their football seats outright like real
estate it's going to be more expensive
to buy than rent at least up front in
the NFL's newest stadium in San
Francisco fans paid as much as eighty
thousand dollars a seat seats in
Minneapolis will be going for a lot less
no more than ten thousand dollars but
fans can expect to pay an average of
twenty five hundred dollars each to get
Viking seats as soon as next year and
there's a catch the license won't get
you into a game
fans will still have to buy tickets from
the Vikings every year to match their
seats think of tickets as the
Association fee for seats above and
beyond the mortgage and taxes
there are advantages and disadvantages
of a seed license plan for fans the big
drawback is that it's very expensive and
fans will have to come up with the money
before the stadium opens the Vikings
owners will use that money to pay for
their half of the billion-dollar stadium
and there's another catch for fans
buying a seed license is a long-term
proposition
the Vikings hoped that paying thousands
of dollars for a seat will keep people
coming to the stadium instead of
watching the games on TV but fans do get
something in return for their money
they'll have title to a seat and they
can sell or trade or give that seat to
someone just like they would with
regular real estate they can get at
least some of their money back and with
some teams the licenses have grown in
value by a lot fans will also be
guaranteed tickets and that may be the
true value that will get ticket holders
in on the ground floor of the secondary
ticket market an industry the state of
Minnesota sanctioned in 2007 when it
legalized scalping big markups for big
games like playoffs or Green Bay
matchups for instance could offset the
cost of seed licenses for fans willing
to sell off some tickets will Vikings
fans go for this scheme if other NFL
cities are any indication they probably
will fans have paid football teams more
than a billion dollars for the seed
licenses in just the last three years
Tim Nelson Minnesota Public Radio News

metadata.title: How NFL Teams Make Money Before Selling Season Tickets ($750 to $50,000 Just for the Right)
metadata.author: THE MARKUP FILES
metadata.shortDescription:
Imagine paying $50,000 for an NFL stadium seat — and finding out your season tickets aren't even included.

That's exactly how Personal Seat Licenses (PSLs) work. And for the Buffalo Bills' new Highmark Stadium, this business model helped generate approximately $263 million in reported fan contributions before the stadium hosted its first NFL game.

But what exactly are fans paying for?

In this episode of The Markup Files, we break down the hidden economics of NFL Personal Seat Licenses — a system that allows football teams to charge fans for the right to purchase season tickets, with the tickets themselves sold separately.

At Buffalo's new $2.1 billion stadium, PSL prices ranged from $750 to an astonishing $50,000 per seat. More than 53,000 licenses were sold, creating a major source of stadium financing.

But the real business model goes deeper than those numbers.

We explore how NFL teams turn fan loyalty into upfront stadium funding, why some seats command extraordinary license fees, how PSL resale marketplaces operate, and what happens when fans want to sell their rights.

We also examine the financial risks for fans, the role of taxpayer funding, and why a seat license can cost thousands of dollars without including admission to a single game.

The biggest question isn't why football tickets are expensive. It's how NFL teams make money before selling the tickets themselves.

Welcome to The Markup Files, where we uncover the business models, hidden costs, and financial systems behind everyday industries.

Research references: Buffalo Bills official stadium announcements, NFL/AP reporting on stadium financing, Pollstar industry reporting, and official PSL marketplace documentation.

This video is an independent educational analysis and is not affiliated with the NFL or the Buffalo Bills.

#NFL #BuffaloBills #TheMarkupFiles

Their FAQ also states clearly that the listing price covers only the licenses, not the tickets, and that the buyer becomes the season ticket holder for all future seasons at those seats. The Bills own resale terms are governed by their specific agreements. The Raiders and Jets examples give us a clear picture of how these programs function at the transaction level. But, the Bills precise terms may differ. Different teams, different contracts. This is why the price shown in a resale listing is not the same as a guaranteed payout. A seller first needs a buyer willing to pay that amount. Then, any applicable marketplace fees, unpaid balances, and transfer conditions can change what the seller walks away with. The new buyer also needs to consider the season ticket bill that follows the license. A seat license can be transferable without being easy to sell, and even a completed sale may leave its original owner with a loss. As for whether PSL values go up or down over time, that depends on things no one can predict with confidence. Demand for those specific seats, how the team performs over the coming years, what ticket prices look like in future seasons, whether the next generation of local fans values season access as at the the current generation paid. A PSL at a thriving franchise in a strong market can be worth more than the original price down the road. In other circumstances, it can be worth less. What matters for the team's finances is that the original proceeds are collected either way. There is no guaranteed return for the buyer, and the value of any PSL depends heavily on what has happened to the franchise and the market by the time the holder needs or wants to sell. Let's put some concrete numbers around the total fan experience because the full picture looks different once you add everything together. This is a hypothetical example using clearly rounded figures. None of these are official Bills prices. Imagine two fans, Mark and Sarah. Together, they purchase two PSLs, one for each seat. At a hypothetical price of $25,000 per seat, their combined license price is $50,000. They might pay the full amount upfront or use an available payment arrangement, which could involve additional costs depending on its terms. Now add the annual ticket cost. If the hypothetical face value of each seat comes to $5,000 per season, that's $10,000 per year for both seats combined. After five seasons, Mark and Sarah have spent $50,000 on PSLs and $50,000 on tickets. A combined $100,000 before parking, food, or any financing charges on the original license. The distinction matters. The PSL is a one-time commitment. The season tickets are a recurring annual cost. The team collected the PSL payment at the time of purchase or through the financing arrangement. It collects the annual ticket revenue separately every season. Two separate transactions, two separate payment streams. Same two seats. If Mark and Sarah eventually decide to sell their licenses, the amount they recover will depend on market demand, their remaining financial obligations, and the specific terms of their Bills license agreement. A resale right does not guarantee they will recover what they originally paid. The team's business runs on both revenue streams from the same seat. A large upfront commitment from the license and steady annual revenue from ticket renewals. The fans' financial exposure is front-loaded in a way that a standard season ticket relationship never was. This is the core trade-off of the model and it plays out differently for everyone involved. For the team and the stadium project, PSL proceeds deliver construction period financing directly from the fan base. That reduces how much the owners need to borrow from commercial lenders at market rates and gives the private side of the project a committed funding source years before the doors open. For the fans, the exchange is this. You're paying today for priority access to specific season tickets as long as you continue meeting the terms of the license agreement. In a market where Bill's season tickets have historically been extremely hard to come by, that kind of locked-in access has real value to the people who want it. The tiered pricing model made it accessible across a wide range of financial situations. $750 for the fan who wants to be in the building, 50,000 for the fan who wants to be in the best seat in it. According to the executive who ran PSL sales for the project, the Bills retained roughly 70 to 75% of their existing season ticket holders through the PSL transition. The highest conversion rate that company had seen on any new NFL stadium build. But the fan carries real financial risk. You're committing money today to a future product whose annual price is set by the team. The resale market reflects conditions at the moment you need to sell, not what you originally paid. And the annual ticket cost continues as long as you hold the license. For the public stakeholders who contributed $850 million to the construction, the deal came with a 30-year lease and a non-relocation clause. The team repays all public funding if it leaves within the first 14 years. The PSL proceeds helped make the private side contribution viable, which is part of what made the overall partnership financially possible. Now, return to where should we started. A fan at the new Highmark Stadium paid $50,000 for the contractual right connected to one premium seat. Not a ticket. Not the chair. The right to be the person who buys the ticket every year for that specific location. The season ticket for that seat is still billed separately. Apply that same idea across more than 53,000 licensed seats with prices ranging from $750 to $50,000 per seat and you get approximately $263 million in reported PSL contributions. Those licenses were sold before the stadium hosted its first NFL game, though some fans paid through financing arrangements rather than handing over the entire amount at once. That is what a PSL actually is. Not a ticket. Not a seat. A contractual right to a transaction that hasn't happened yet. Priced, sold, and applied to construction financing before the thing being sold even existed. NFL teams don't just sell the experience of watching football. Some of them sell the right to buy that experience. And as it turns out, that right, the right itself, is worth quite a lot to the people who want it.

metadata.title: Why Football Stadiums Are Turning Into Luxury Hotels
metadata.author: SportsRender
metadata.shortDescription:
Football stadiums are changing, and not just on the pitch.

In many modern venues, traditional seats are quietly being replaced by luxury suites, VIP boxes, and premium hospitality spaces that look more like hotel rooms than stadium seating. Some of these suites now include private lounges, fine dining, floor-to-ceiling glass views, and even overnight experiences overlooking the pitch.
For clubs, the reason is simple: one luxury suite can generate more revenue than dozens of regular seats.
From a business perspective, it makes sense.

In this video we explore how luxury hospitality is transforming modern football stadiums, why clubs are investing heavily in VIP experiences, and what this might mean for the future of the matchday atmosphere.

instead of sitting on a plastic seat in
the stands, you're lying on a king-size
bed. There's champagne on the table.

bathtubs.
And the match?

For a long time, stadiums followed one
simple rule.
Fit as many fans as possible inside the
building. More seats meant more tickets.
More fans meant more atmosphere.
But in modern stadium design, the logic
is starting to change.

how many people they can fit inside.

money each seat can generate. And that
small shift is changing how stadiums are
built.

and more areas are being turned into

apartments inside a stadium.

walls, private dining areas, lounge
furniture, climate-controlled rooms.
Some even have beds and private
bathrooms.
Honestly, some of them feel closer to a
hotel room than a football seat.
And here's the big difference compared
to the past. These spaces aren't built
just for match days anymore.
Clubs want their stadiums to be active
all year round.
Suites can host business meetings,
private parties, corporate events.
Some venues even offer overnight
experiences with views of the pitch.
So, the stadium becomes something bigger
than a place to watch football. It
becomes an entertainment venue 365
days a year.
From the club's perspective, this
strategy makes a lot of sense. A single
premium suite can bring in tens of
thousands, sometimes even hundreds of
thousands, per season.
And that might come from just one
client. Usually large companies,
sponsors, or very wealthy fans.
In other words, the stadium becomes a
piece of premium real estate.
The view of the pitch is the product.
And the match, well, sometimes it almost
becomes the background.
Clubs like Real Madrid have pushed this
model very far.
After the huge renovation of the
Santiago Bernabéu, premium hospitality
became a major part of the stadium's
business model.
Between VIP seating, events, and
concerts, the stadium now generates
revenue far beyond just football
matches.
But, there is a catch. Because every
luxury suite usually replaces dozens of
regular seats.
And that means fewer traditional fans
inside the stadium.
You've probably seen it during
broadcasts. The camera shows a luxury
box and half the people inside are
looking at their phones.
Meanwhile, the real noise is coming from
the stands. Down near the pitch, fans
are chanting and singing.
Up in the suites, it's often quieter,
more private, more relaxed. It's almost
like two completely different stadium
experiences happening at the same time.
And for some supporters, that raises an
uncomfortable question.
Is football slowly becoming less about
the crowd and more about premium
hospitality?
And this trend isn't slowing down.
Modern venues like Tottenham Hotspur
Stadium helped set a new standard for
hospitality-focused design.
Now, clubs across Europe and North
America are following the same idea.
Future stadiums are increasingly
designed as mixed-use entertainment
complexes.
Inside the same building, you might find
restaurants, event spaces, offices,
hotels.
In some cases, people might even stay
overnight inside the stadium itself,
which is something that would have
sounded impossible just a few years ago.
Personally, I think clubs are walking a
very thin line here.
On one side, these luxury spaces bring
in huge revenue, money that helps teams
compete at the highest level.
But on the other side, stadiums have
always been about the fans and the
atmosphere they create.
And if too many traditional seats
disappear, something important could be
lost.
So, what do you think?
Is this just smart business for modern
football, or are stadiums slowly losing
part of their identity?
Let me know your thoughts in the
comments.
And if you enjoy exploring stadium
design, architecture, and the business
behind modern football venues, make sure
to subscribe to Sports Render.
Thanks for watching and I'll see you in

segments.text: It's easily something that we've done in food and beverage and in hotels but
is kind of new here in the NFL.
I am going into my third season with the Vikings.
I came from a strong hotel background with seven years
with Walt Disney World at the Grand Floridian Resort and Spa,
three years with Hilton Orlando, and three years with Marriott.
I got this position because the Vikings were trying to do something different with their service initiatives,
and wanted to model our department after a hotel setup.
Because I don't have a sports background, I bring in a lot of weird, outside ideas.
Some of them are crazy, but some of them have been really well received and
kind of blend over from hotels into football really well.
Just this season, we started our Minnesota Vikings Black Jacket program,
which is essentially like a Maitre D' program in our suite corridors.
So we have professional folks that are just wanting to provide ultimate service to our suite guests,
and they greet our suite guests when they enter the corridor,
and then just like a high-end restaurant, escort them into their suite.
But on that walk, that's where they make the connection.
So they introduce themselves, they ask them where they're traveling from,
they tell these guests who our pre-show entertainment is, our halftime entertainment.
But before the game, we distribute what we call 'Purple Notes' to all of our suite Black Jackets.
They read the Purple Notes, so they have talking points to prepare themselves for that walk.
That walk is really important.
And then during the game, they pop into assigned suites and do a first half suite visit,
a second half suite visit, and then they just position themselves in the corridor
so that they're ready and willing to assist with any guests' needs -
Where's the ATM? Oh my gosh, my grandmother locked her keys in the car,
how do I get to the Fleet Farm (Parking) Ramp from here?
And then they're prepared to walk them there.
It's a VIP experience that is so simple and has hit a home run with our suite guests.
They're never scared to ask a question,
and they're always comfortable going to the Vikings Black Jackets with anything that they may need.
So that has just excelled perfectly in this kind of situation.
It's easily something that we've done in food and beverage and in hotels,
but it's kind of new here in the NFL, so it's been a home run.
Another thing that we've done is my department wants to know more about
who the clients are that are in the suites.
So very simple, we send out an email the Monday or Tuesday before a home game,
and it's two fields. It's literally 'Who is hosting your suite for this game?'
And 'Tell us about the clientele in your suite?'
We populate it to a spreadsheet, add it to the Purple Notes, and now our Black Jackets are prepared.
They know who they're looking for in every suite that they walk into and
if that suite is trying to close a $2 million deal, or if they're there to party.
Whatever it may be, now they know the tone that is set in that suite,
and that has also hit a home run with our suite clients as well.
ALSD has been awesome for us because we've met so many people throughout
the professional sports community that are doing the same things that we're trying to do.
We're all trying to get better.
We're all trying to be the best, either in our cities or our organizations, whatever it may be.
It's a forum where we all get to network, and come together, and share crazy ideas, failures, successes,
make friends in the same community.
And then through that, it's gone throughout the year.
There's probably 12 of us that are part of an email string where we just share ideas like,
'Hey guys, I'm halfway through the season. I need some refreshed ideas.'
And there's 12 of us from the NFL that just constantly share ideas,
and it's because of ALSD that we're work friends,
we're professional contacts, and now we're idea sharers.

Es algo que no había pensado de que me tenía que poner a guardarme sitio para mí mismo porque si no no vería la carrera de ninguna manera desde la barandilla. Y ya estáis viendo que va a estar bastante complicado. Y bueno, como podéis ver en estas imágenes, se disfrutó muchísimo. Todo el espectáculo previo antes de la salida de este Gran Premio de los Países Bajos pude ver la salida de manera más o menos bien, pero a partir de ahí pues fue un poco lo que me temía. Tuve que buscar asiento, tuve que buscar un monitor para poder seguir la acción de la carrera porque desde la barandilla era misión imposible. A partir de ahí, pues no grabé gran cosa porque estaba concentrado siguiendo la carrera. No soy el típico que se graba sus reacciones viendo un Gran Premio. Entonces estuve ahí degustando esa locura con un safety car con otro. La grada se ponía de pie, gritaba a la mínima que había algún incidente. Durante algunos momentos fue una experiencia bastante deprimente siendo español, viendo cómo le estaba yendo tanto a Fernando Alonso como a Carlos Sainz. Y bueno, como ya podéis imaginar, en el tramo final de esta carrera, hubo un momento en el que se hizo el silencio en mi zona del Pado Club porque el McLaren de Lando Norris se había quedado fuera de carrera, pero por lo menos fue Óscar Piastri, el otro de los dos McLaren quien impudo llevarse la victoria y llevarse 25 puntos para casa. Pues bueno, se acabó el Gran Premio, se acabó la experiencia del Padok Club del Gran Premio de los Países Bajos 2025, penúltimo Gran Premio seguramente en muchísimo tiempo de los Países Bajos y y la verdad que tengo sensaciones encontradas, o sea, no quiero parecer poco agradecido. La experiencia, por una parte, ha sido absolutamente descomunal el poder eh ver la Fórmula 1 desde un lugar como este, desde una posición tan privilegiada. todo lo que es la comida, también la atención del enorme equipo que gestiona todo esto del Padoclub, la verdad que es algo absolutamente descomunal y es una experiencia totalmente inolvidable, especialmente ese momento de entrar en el pit lane, ¿no? Yo en el pit lane he entrado algunas veces, he estado incluso durante sesiones como fotógrafo, recordaréis las batallitas en Mónaco 2018 y todas estas cosas, pero nunca en un momento así, en un domingo, a menos de 2 horas del arranque de un Gran Premio de Fórmula 1 repleto de gente. La verdad que ha sido una sensación absolutamente alucinante. Alucinante. Se queda corto. Pero sí que es cierto que me he quedado un poco mosca con la experiencia de cómo se vive la carrera desde aquí. Seguramente si os tuviese que recomendar venir al Pad Club, que si os sobra una ingente cantidad de dinero, por supuesto que os lo recomiendo, supongo. Casi que os recomendaría más venir el viernes o el sábado y no venir el domingo, más que nada porque yo, pues claro, luego se dice muchísimo esto de que no, la gente que va al Pado Club va por la experiencia, le da igual la carrera y puedo entender por qué le puede dar igual la carrera porque desde aquí es difícil verla. Por supuesto que dentro hay muchísimos monitores, muchísimos puntos para seguir la carrera con el sofá y con todo, pero fuera es complicado, pues porque está esta barandilla y no hay ninguna silla, no hay ninguna como especie de grada especial solamente para el pado club, donde cada uno tiene asegurado un buen punto de vista de del circuito. Y claro, a mí me ha pillado por sorpresa. Yo pensaba que en el pado club no tendría que hacer como en la peluz de Monmeló, que tienes que madrugar y tienes que pillar barandilla pronto porque si no en el momento de arranque de la carrera va a estar toda la gente ocupando la barandilla y no vas a poder ver nada. Además, en este punto del de la recta principal no hay ninguna pantalla tampoco por el otro lado. Por tanto, si te quedas aquí, no ves mucho de la pista y tampoco puedes seguir el resto de la carrera con alguna pantalla que haya eh por aquí detrás. la hay en el vértice, pasado el vértice de la curva uno y es ahí donde finalmente he logrado encontrar un hueco para seguir parte de la acción en alguna resalida de saf car o o alguna historia así. Pero la verdad que ese momento de la verdad, el momento de ver el Gran Premio, pues debido a esto no me ha terminado de molar. Yo pensaba que habría como más ayudas de de visibilidad y demás. Claro, aquí, por ejemplo, yo estoy ahora mismo en una mesilla donde la gente ha estado tomando cosas durante todo el Gran Premio y si estás sentado aquí y la gente está puesta aquí en la barandilla, no ves absolutamente nada. Entonces, eso la verdad que me ha sorprendido un poco porque pues bueno, yo no he abonado el coste de la entrada del del Pado Club. Agradezco muchísimo la invitación, pero si tuviese el dineral que hay que pagar para entrar aquí, por supuesto que la experiencia es irrepetible, es inolvidable, especialmente en los momentos previos, en un circuito como este, donde con toda la grada cantando y y poniendo forma la bandera de los Países Bajos. Pero el momento de la carrera, yo es que quizás soy demasiado friky. Y nada, aquí termina la aventura. Yo no sé muy bien cómo quedará este vídeo, la verdad, porque lo he ido grabando como improvisando mucho porque te ibas moviendo de un sitio para otro e iba descubriendo 1000 mundos aquí dentro del recinto del Padok Club. Entonces ha sido como un efectivamente un niño pequeño descubriendo eh el lujo de de la Fórmula 1 desde dentro. Entonces creo que el vídeo se verá bastante así, bastante amater, bastante de chaval de pueblo de repente viniendo a la élite. Pero bueno, yo he disfrutado muchísimo de esta experiencia y espero que vosotros también. Desde luego es un vídeo distinto, es un vídeo que no es tan habitual. De nuevo, muchísimas gracias por traerme aquí y por hacerme vivir esta experiencia y espero que lo hayáis disfrutado también vosotros desde vuestras casas. Esto ha sido todo por hoy. Si te gustó el vídeo, pon un me gusta y deja un comentario. Un saludo.

metadata.title: Is the F1 Paddock Club Actually Worth It?
metadata.author: Kayvan Goes
metadata.shortDescription:
I spent a full day at the Formula 1 Paddock Club during the Dutch Grand Prix and decided to break down the entire experience honestly, category by category.

In this video, I review the Paddock Club based on:

• Tickets & Arrival
• Production
• Entertainment
• Food & Hospitality
• Staff
• Networking
• Uniqueness
• Venue
• Overall Experience
• Atmosphere
• How memorable it actually was

And not everything scored highly.

For example, networking got just 1/10, while entertainment scored 4/10. So while the F1 Paddock Club looks incredible from the outside, I wanted to talk about what the experience is actually like when you're there and whether I think it's worth the money.

More behind the scenes on my instagram: https://www.instagram.com/kayvan_experience/

This isn't an F1 expert review. It's simply my perspective as someone who attends a lot of premium events and experiences around the world.

If you want to actually see what the day looked like  the Paddock Club, food, hospitality, racing, atmosphere and everything that happened  watch my full vlog here on the channel.

If you've been to the F1 Paddock Club, I'd also love to hear your experience in the comments. Did you agree with my scores?

metadata.title: The VIP Experience | How It Works: F1 Hospitality 🤩
metadata.author: Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team
metadata.shortDescription:
Our Hospitality and Events programmes provide an unforgettable experience for our partners and guests at every F1 race, thanks to the relentless work of our Marketing team.
Hospitality is something that often flies under the radar. Working seamlessly in the background while people enjoy the experience put in front of them. But it requires a lot of preparation and quick-thinking on the ground to deliver the best programme possible at every race we visit.

Don't forget to like, subscribe and hit the notification bell to make sure you never miss any of our videos! 👉 http://bit.ly/12EFRRD

http://www.MercedesAMGF1.com

http://instagram.com/MercedesAMGF1

https://www.tiktok.com/@mercedesamgf1

https://www.facebook.com/MercedesAMGF1

https://twitter.com/MercedesAMGF1

#F1 #MercedesAMGF1

segments.text: Hi, my name is Victoria Johnson. I'm
marketing operations director for the
Mercedes AMG Petronas Formula 1 team.
The overall goal of our hospitality
program is to be the best in world
sport. Hospitality and events is
integral to our sponsorship platform. It
provides our shareholders and our
partners a platform to invite C-level
guests, current potential customers. It
also allows us and them to invite
A-listers and influencers to the races.
Hi, I'm Sarah Morgan. I'm the head of
hospitality and events here at the
Mercedes AMG Petronas Formula 1 team.
Some of our experiences we offer to our
guests when they're with us at a race
range from private garage tours hosted
by our amazing verbal team. They know
more about F1 than anyone I've ever met
in my life. We also offer private
viewing galleries where our guests can
sit at the back of the garage during the
race and really be a part of the live
action. We're very fortunate as the
Mercedes brand to draw a large crowd of
A-listers and celebrities to our races
as well. Not to mention our incredible
drivers are very well connected to a lot
of great celebs. So, we get the pleasure
of hosting these guys in the garage, in
the motor home, and from time to time in
our paddock club as well. People from
Tom Cruise to Queen Latifah, Roger
Federer, and the list goes on and we're
always super thrilled to have them at
track. Mercedes Benz brand is the eighth
largest brand in the world and its
philosophy is all around luxury and best
in class. We try and take that forward
into all of our hospitality and events.
The Mercedes experience for us, it's a
unique experience. It's like being part
of a special club, a part of a family
and that's how we pride ourselves. Our
hospitality is to the highest standard
but in a very relaxed effortless way. I
have a team of 10 people on my
hospitality and events team that operate
everything to do with hospitality at the
company.
I have a core team of people from
designers to project managers to
hospitality and event specialists and
they all come together to deliver these
phenomenal experiences. Hospitality can
add to performance of the team in many
ways.
We ensure that the team has a relaxed
comfortable environment to work in and
to be successful in. It also allows us
to host our existing partners and ensure
they have an amazing time and want to
resign and join us again for future
years. It also allows our commercial
team to bring in prospects and ensure
that they're going to have an absolutely
seamless VIP top-notch experience.
Hospitality and events gives us a
platform to illustrate our brand and our
brand standards. It provides us an
opportunity to showcase Mercedes-Benz
and also showcase our portfolio of
partners. Also putting a little bit of
our team identity in. So the creative
process for all of our spaces starts
more than a year out if you can believe
it from races and events. We have three
different kits that travel around the
world to cater to the different spaces,
different sizes and different needs of
every race. We also have additional kit
for exceptional races such as Monaco
which require a totally different kit
and set up. So the process is long and
very technical.
We work very closely with the design and
production teams to ensure that we're
delivering top-notch hospitality
experiences in line with our brand
ambition and in a beautiful space. So
we're doing quite a lot of exceptional
hospitality this year and in coming
years. First and foremost being our
Monaco operation where we operate not
our standard paddock club but an
apartment private apartment penthouse, a
private yacht and a huge paddock program
as well. So this requires a a different
set of equipment and team to operate and
manage. The logistics are huge. We're
also trying to implement ongoing
trackside hospitality at some of the new
big races such as Miami and Vegas. This
year in Miami, we did for the second
time our Miami Club, which is a huge
trackside operation that can house up to
850 people with live DJs, live
entertainment, and a whole bunch of
exciting action. So, 2023 saw our second
edition of the Miami Club. This club was
born out of a need for more space for
our existing partners to host more
guests. The demand was just too strong,
so we needed another space. We're able
to offer live DJs, driver appearances,
and incredible trackside views of the
race. For the first time in 2023, we
will see a Formula 1 race come to Vegas.
So, we will have our Vegas Club situated
on turn four that can hold up to 850
guests. This is going to be the best in
class hospitality with top-notch
catering, local entertainment that you
only get to see at private shows
normally in Vegas. We'll have live DJs,
international DJs, and also the chance
to see drivers come and do a driver
appearance. The club will span over
three floors with each floor having a
totally different theme and vibe with
different opportunities on every floor
to see exciting entertainment and
experience different cuisine. The Vegas
Club gives us the opportunity to
showcase to our partners and their
guests why we at Mercedes are best in
class at what we do.
We've had some real successes with our
Miami Club, and we're now going to take
that forward into the Vegas Club this
year.
We have created a great platform, a
great look and feel. We have started to
identify different areas of
entertainment, but we want to push
ourselves further, and hopefully Vegas
Club at the end of the year will be a
step towards that. Hospitality and
events is a huge opportunity for us to
stay ahead of the competition. Formula 1
is evolving at a really, really fast
pace and therefore we will continue to
invest and involve our hospitality and
events platform. We've created this
special set of clubs with Vegas Club and
Miami Club and we're going to further
extend that out to Silverstone and
Singapore next year. We're collaborating
with the Ritz-Carlton on their
Ritz-Carlton yacht, which will be in
Monaco next year. We're always looking
for that extra thing we can do to
deliver a unique experience to our
partners. Our hospitality and events
take a huge amount of hours of hard
work. Watching them come to life, the
attention to detail and the seamless
delivery is one of the best feelings in
the world.

metadata.title: I Upgraded My F1 Ticket In China…
metadata.author: Live The Dash
metadata.shortDescription:
LUXURY Formula 1 Experience in China 🇨🇳 
Shanghai Grand Prix + Paddock Club + 5⭐ Hotel + Business Class Train

Ever wondered what it’s like to experience Formula 1 at the highest level of luxury? I
n this video, I take you along to the incredible Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai — but not from the regular grandstands. This is the ultimate F1 experience inside the Formula 1 Paddock Club.

From VIP trackside views and world-class hospitality to exclusive pit lane walks, this is how the elite watch Formula 1.

But the luxury didn’t stop at the circuit. The entire trip was designed to be unforgettable:
✨ Upgraded business class train travel in China
🏨 5-star stay at the W Hotel Shanghai with an iconic Bund skyline view
🍾 Premium food, champagne, and hospitality inside the F1 Paddock Club
🏎️ Front-row access to the world’s fastest sport

If you’ve ever dreamed of attending a Formula 1 Grand Prix in true VIP style, this video shows exactly what it’s like — from arrival in Shanghai to race day inside the most exclusive area of the track.

Expect behind-the-scenes moments, luxury travel, incredible views of the race, and the full Formula 1 lifestyle experience.

🏁 In this video you'll see:

What the F1 Paddock Club experience is really like
Inside the Shanghai International Circuit during race weekend
Luxury travel across China by business class high-speed train
My stay at the W Shanghai – The Bund with skyline views
Incredible F1 race moments and trackside atmosphere

📍 Location: Shanghai, China
🏎️ Event: Formula 1 Chinese Grand Prix
🎟️ Ticket: F1 Paddock Club VIP Hospitality

If you love Formula 1, luxury travel, or motorsport experiences, don’t forget to:

Comment your favourite F1 track!
 --------------------------------------------

“Small Budgets Can Stretch Many Miles"

 --------------------------------------------

Inquiries: ryanjadedash@gmail.com

metadata.author: Katarina Mogus
metadata.shortDescription:
I got the chance to experience Formula 1 in a way I never imagined... with VIP access to Ferrari at the Canadian Grand Prix in Montreal. 🏎️🇨🇦

From the Ferrari garage and paddock to incredible trackside views, luxury hospitality, and behind-the-scenes moments,  this was one of the most unforgettable experiences I've ever had.

Come along as I take you inside the world of Formula 1 and show you what it's really like to a spend race weekend.

✨ Ferrari VIP hospitality

metadata.shortDescription:
I got invited into the McLaren Paddock Club at Silverstone and somehow ended up inside the garage during a live session. This is what F1's top table actually looks like.

Climb the ladder with me on Patreon: https://patreon.com/lawvs

Thanks to Jon, my pal from Airwallex (a McLaren sponsor), I upped the ante at Silverstone this time. With my paddock club wristband on, I did the pit lane walk, got up close to McLaren's special livery for the British GP and ate the world's fanciest buffet.

And oh yes, I also attempted, for the second time, to actually speak to Mika Hakkinen. You can guess how that went.

metadata.title: Inside Club Magnolia: The Masters’ secret experience with Atlanta ties
metadata.author: CBS Atlanta
metadata.shortDescription: Just outside Augusta National, Club Magnolia offers a hidden Masters experience powered by connections to metro Atlanta. Go inside the exclusive club with Daniel Wilkerson to see how Atlanta chefs and hospitality shape this unique tradition, open only seven days a year.

metadata.title: $2900 World Cup VIP Hospitality ticket! Am I crazy?
metadata.author: Travel with Frodo
metadata.shortDescription:
Today I'll be going to my first ever world cup match between Qatar and Switzerland at Levis Stadium in the San Francisco Bay Area! I bought a VIP hospitality ticket for a crazy $2900! What did I get for my money? I'll show the lounge area, food, seat, and gift that you get for this ticket.

#worldcup #travel  #luxurytravel

segments.text: Hello, and a warm welcome to the
channel. Thank you for joining me, and
today I have something really special.
[music]
I'll be attending my first ever World
Cup football match.
My ticket cost me a whopping $2,900.
[music] So, please like and subscribe if
you like this video to help me pay off
the credit card bill.
I have no idea what I'm getting for the
money. So, without further ado, let's
go.
It's 8:36 in the morning in the San
Francisco Bay Area in sunny California,
and I just left the Hyatt Regency Santa
Clara, and I'm walking towards Levi's
Stadium where Qatar will be playing
against Switzerland. It's only a
10-minute walk to the stadium, so it's
really handy to stay at the Hyatt. The
gates open at 9:00 a.m., so I wanted to
get there as soon as I could and
maximize my time there. And kickoff will
be at 12:00, so I'll have a few hours to
relax.
There are already a ton of people here,
but there are lots of gates, so each
individual queue is not too bad at the
moment. There are four levels of
hospitality tickets available, and I
bought the VIP ticket, the second most
expensive one 9 months ago for $2,900.
The FIFA website has brief descriptions
of what each ticket offers, but it's not
that clear, and I really wasn't sure
what I would get.
My ticket includes VIP entry, but I
don't see any specific queue for
hospitality.
They provide some links that show the
stadium and entrances, and it does say
there is a VIP entrance to the side, but
the area I'm heading to is in the front,
and that's the gate that my ticket says
to use, so it's a bit confusing. There
are lots of FIFA officials in yellow
shirts hanging around to answer any
questions, and I asked them, but they
didn't really know, and it seemed like
just waiting here would be best. Since
the queue is not that long at the
moment, that's what I'm doing. At 9:20,
the gates opened.
Here you can see the security check
right after the gate.
That didn't take long, and I was soon
inside.
The first thing I did was head to the
Bank of America fan zone area.
The queue is already quite long, and I
had to wait maybe 10 minutes. They offer
some free bracelets, and they look
pretty good. This is an American one and
a San Francisco one. The San Francisco
one is pretty cool with a sea lion from
Fisherman's Wharf, the iconic Golden
Gate Bridge, and a cable car from
downtown.
Now I'm in the line for the FIFA store.
I actually didn't bother waiting here. I
left soon after as there wasn't anything
that interesting in the store for me.
I'm finally in the hospitality area with
a welcome champagne on arrival. You can
see it's a really nice setup.
There are lots of tables, chairs, TVs,
and then through the large glass windows
you can see the stadium and even the
pitch. I'm very impressed with the
location. It's really [music] great and
right in the middle of the action so you
can soak up all the atmosphere in the
comfort of the lounge area.
>> [music]
>> There are some fridges around which
contain lots of bottled water and Coke.
And then there is this large bar area in
the middle with lots of alcoholic and
soft drinks.
However, strangely there are no hot
drinks available. So no coffee and no
tea even though it's before 10:00 in the
morning. There isn't even hot water
available. This is really disappointing.
Here you can see the chef stations at
the end and all the food is located
here.
There is a similar setup on the other
end with the same food is duplicated.
They actually have a small store here
that says you haven't to wait in line
outside.
There was never much of a queue here so
it's a great perk to have this here.
Here is the menu for today.
Unfortunately, even though it's
breakfast time, there are only lunch
items and no breakfast available.
I was expecting to have breakfast at
this time and then thinking they would
switch over to lunch items. Perhaps I've
been spoiled with Formula 1 hospitality
which does offer breakfast and lunch.
Or maybe I should have got the more
expensive ticket.
Comment below if you think I'm expecting
too much.
It's not a huge amount of items and the
mains do look a bit suspect but they
have burgers and that's really all I
need to fill up on.
Here are the snack items available.
Dill pickle popcorn,
olives, salt pepper dew peppers, nuts.
Crudite and dips.
Cheese.
Here are the desserts. [music]
Berry shortbread trifle.
Fresh fruit and berries.
Baklava, cookies, brownies, bars, and
macarons.
Here is my first plate. I have the
burger, macaroni cheese, quesadilla, and
tri tip.
They have a few more items that aren't
on the menu, like the macaroni cheese
and some large chicken pieces, which I
did not get.
The quesadilla is pretty good. It's been
sitting there for a while, but the
tortilla is soft and there's a good
amount of cheese inside.
The tri tip is medium rare and a bit
chewy. I think in general, I prefer my
meat more cooked, even though I know
it's not proper.
It's nice that they have some creamy
horseradish, though.
This burger is really nice, though. The
bun looks like a football, which is
pretty cool, and it's really tasty.
The meat is mostly well done, and you
can see a little cheese here. There are
[music] also caramelized onions, which
have a really nice sweetness, almost
like an onion jam.
For my second plate, I have some salad,
creamed spinach, and more tri tip.
The salad is very fresh and the leaves
are tasty.
The creamed spinach is pretty decent.
I got this food from the chef stations
at the other end. And you can see the
tri tip is more well done.
I really like this one. It's still
tender, but it has better flavor and is
not chewy at all.
This is really good.
These entertainers appeared at this
point. They weren't announced or
anything.
I just happened to see them while I was
eating.
It was nice to see them perform, but I
don't know if they're part of one of the
countries playing or just random
entertainment.
Here is my next plate, and I have
another burger, the fried cheese
ravioli, and a chicken [music] skewer.
A waiter was walking around with a plate
of chicken skewers, so I thought I'd
give it a go.
It's a little spicy, but quite tasty.
It's still juicy, even though I think
it's been out for a bit.
The ravioli is really disappointing for
me. [music]
It's supposedly the main course, but
there's really nothing.
The outer edge is quite hard, but at
least the cheese inside is soft. [music]
I would prefer if it was just normal
ravioli.
I think it was even labeled as just
fried cheese.
The burger is great, but it's a little
different to the first one.
It's just a normal bun, not the
football-shaped one.
And the bun doesn't taste as good,
especially since it's not been toasted.
However, this tastes a bit more creamy
than the other one. [music]
And I think maybe it has a little more
cheese or a different cheese, so it's
actually really enjoyable and tastes
different than the first burger.
It's now an hour to kick off, and I
found out that there's another FIFA
shop. So, I went out to have a look. But
of course, there's a massive queue, so I
didn't bother and just turned back.
If you want merchandise, I recommend
going first thing.
It's definitely pretty busy though, and
pretty much all [music] the seats are
taken.
Always good to come early so you can get
your spot.
Some people are starting to appear in
the stadium, but I think the rest of
them are still queuing up for all the
activities outside.
I went for dessert, but the brownies and
bars are already gone.
They really shouldn't run out so quickly
on these basic items.
This is the berry shortbread trifle and
baklava.
The baklava is well made [music] and the
pastry is good. I just don't eat
baklava, so it's not my thing.
The trifle is pretty good. It's pretty
and very tasty.
The opening ceremony has started, and
wow, just look at how good these seats
are.
I'm in row 15, so I'm really close to
the pitch, which is really cool.
The seat is pretty comfy. I had no
trouble with legroom or the width of the
seat.
Having said that, there were no one to
the right of me, so you never know.
The atmosphere is just incredible. You
are surrounded by passionate fans
everywhere, and even though there are
some opposing fans mixed around,
everyone is really friendly.
Unfortunately, there is no shade here
and it's really sunny. So, be sure to
bring a hat and sunscreen.
You can see a big white section of
supporters and they are the Qatar
supporters dressed in their white robes
called a thobe.
There is a similar red Swiss section on
the other side.
You can see the players are walking onto
the pitch now.
I'm so close I can actually read the
names on their shirts. It's crazy.
The big TVs are easy to see for the
score and the time remaining and also
for replays.
>> [music]
>> So, you can't of course replay the live
action in front of you.
Time for kickoff and we are underway.
It's incredible to watch this in real
life.
I watched many games on the telly and I
have to say it's completely different in
real life.
On the telly, the pitch seems huge but
here in person, the pitch actually looks
quite small.
It's almost like I'm at a school event
watching a casual game.
This is very similar to how Wimbledon
was. I was at number one court and it
felt so much smaller in person than how
I remember watching it on the telly.
It's only been 15 minutes and it's
already a penalty.
You can feel the anticipation in the
air.
>> [cheering]
>> And it's a goal.
I guess there are a lot of Swiss
supporters around me. It's really
amazing to be in this crowd as they
celebrate.
During the start of the second half, I
popped down to the store and sure enough
there was no queue to get in.

have team jerseys for Qatar and
Switzerland. But unfortunately, no
jerseys for other teams.
That's really disappointing. I was
hoping to snag a Scotland jersey.
Qatar scored right at the end and spot
the Qatar supporter in the sea of red.
But that's football.
The Swiss supporters are really
dejected. But on the other side of the

The hospitality is open for 2 hours

All the drinks and food are still
available so you can have a relaxing

It also means you don't have to bother

Instead, you can just sip your champagne

The food is still the same, but some

I got one as well as some more tri-tip.

Statistics show that navigating unfamiliar international venues increases travel fatigue by 40%. By standardizing your experience with a hospitality partner, you maintain a consistent level of accessibility and care, whether you're in the humidity of Miami or the high altitudes of Mexico City. Finally, what is the single most important safety factor to consider when attending an event of this scale? The sheer scale of a World Cup requires intense security, which can be overwhelming. Hospitality zones offer an integrated security experience where the staff to guest ratio is much higher than in general admission. This provides a much quieter, more controlled environment for entering and exiting the stadium. Having that extra layer of peace of mind allows you to focus entirely on the beautiful game. You aren't worried about the crowds or the logistics. You're simply there to witness history from the best seat in the house. The 2026 World Cup is a milestone event, but it's even more beautiful when viewed with a glass of wine from a padded seat. By choosing hospitality, you aren't just buying a ticket. You're buying a stress-free entry into the world's biggest sporting stage. You've earned the right to see the world. Now make sure you see it in comfort.

metadata.title: This is what it's like to scalp World Cup tickets
metadata.author: Reuters
metadata.shortDescription:
Ticketless FIFA World Cup fans are increasingly gathering at stadium perimeters to haggle with hawkers, pushing tickets for popular matches up to 10 times face value. They seem undeterred by police patrols, CCTV cameras and laws forbidding the practice.

segments.text: Following several complaints from
Ticketmaster users regarding cloning or
fraud when purchasing tickets, the
platform has implemented a new security
measure called Safetix. It is a digital
ticket intended to provide greater
security when purchasing or entering
events, as it features a dynamic code
that changes every 15 seconds. This
problem reached its peak in 2022, when,
upon trying to enter Bad Bunny's
concert, the system notified some users
that their code had already been used.
This caused hundreds of users to be
unable to access the concert, although
they later received a full refund plus
20%compensation. And how can you use
Safetix? To use it, you must follow
these steps. Download the Ticketmaster
MX app on your phone. Log in with your
username and password. Locate the "My
Events" section and find your ticket.
In the Android or iOS Wallet app, you
will find the barcode that must be
scanned at the event entrance. Once at
the event, you must show your ticket on
your phone. It will be scanned, and you
will enter without any setbacks. To use
Safetix more efficiently, you should
take the following steps into account.
Present the dynamic barcode of your
digital ticket in its original size. Do
not make it larger or smaller. Verify
that the elements of your digital
Ticketmaster Safetix are in motion.
Present your phone with no damage to
the screen. Your phone's battery must
be charged, as good brightness and
contrast quality are necessary. If your
phone has an anti-spy screen protector,
you must remove it for the digital
ticket to be read correctly. That is
everything you need to know about
Safetix, the new way to protect your
digital tickets for attending events.
Remember to leave any other topics you
would like to know about in the
comments.

metadata.title: Concert Tickets: Why a 90% Artist Share Misleads
metadata.author: Why It Costs
metadata.shortDescription:
An expensive concert ticket pays through several overlapping businesses. Follow admission, contractual fees, and resale to see why an artist’s majority share does not describe the entire checkout payment.

Thesis: The strongest evidence says a premium concert ticket pays for two overlapping businesses: artist-led admission pricing funds the performance and its production, while contractual ticket fees fund venues and distribution; market power can raise those charges, and resale can divert the premium to a seller outside the show. Counterintuitively, the artist's widely quoted majority share applies after show costs, not to the fan's entire payment, and Live Nation reported a Concerts adjusted operating margin of just 3.3% in 2025 despite record attendance (S1, S2, S4, S5, S6).

metadata.shortDescription:
Concert tickets sell out in minutes, then reappear at higher prices. We break down ticket scalping and the federal case against REPS & Company—a ticket broker accused of using thousands of accounts, VPNs, proxies, and multi-session browsers to bypass Ticketmaster and AXS purchase limits.

Get proxies from Proxxxymiron:
https://proxxxymiron.cc/44703121

According to the lawsuit, between January 2022 and October 2025, the defendants spent more than $1.3 billion buying over 18.5 million tickets and generated at least $120.8 million in resale profit. Tickets were resold through marketplaces including StubHub, Vivid Seats, SeatGeek, and Gametime.

One example involved a single Beyoncé concert. The complaint alleges that REPS used at least 1,300 accounts to purchase 7,624 tickets despite a limit of four to eight per buyer. The alleged resale profit from that concert alone was approximately $833,000.

The operation described in the complaint went far beyond opening extra accounts. It involved different names, email addresses, phone numbers, virtual credit cards, rotating proxies, and separate browser sessions. An internal “Error Bible” reportedly documented Ticketmaster error messages and instructions for working around purchase restrictions.

In this video:

— How ticket scalpers allegedly appeared as thousands of independent buyers
— What proxy servers and multi-session browsers contributed to the operation
— Why REPS maintained a Ticketmaster “Error Bible”
— How an AXS verification check reportedly slowed purchases by 40%
— Why frequent IP changes could trigger account blocks
— Why the company planned to keep the same proxy or IP assigned to each account

00:24 REPS and ticket resale marketplaces

The U.S. Department of Justice filed this civil lawsuit following a referral from the Federal Trade Commission. The conduct described remains allegations; the court has not determined the defendants’ liability.

But what do proxies have to do with any of this? California ticket broker Reps and Company allegedly bypassed the technical restrictions imposed by ticketing platforms and resold tickets to various events through StubHub, Vivid Seats, SeatGeek, GameTime, and other marketplaces. To make this scheme work, the company reportedly used various tools to appear to Ticketmaster and access as thousands of independent buyers. To avoid being blocked, it allegedly used other people's names, numerous email addresses and phone numbers, VPNs, rotating proxies, multi-session browsers, and other methods. The company could create as many as 40 accounts under a single real person's name. They even used a Bible. No, not to get God on their side. They had their own error Bible, which contained Ticketmaster error messages and instructions for bypassing them, allowing employees to keep buying tickets without interruption. Want to buy a ticket to the Beyoncé concert you've dreamed of attending your entire life? Reps got there first and would resell it to you at a markup. The company allegedly made more than 800,000 dollars from tickets to a single Beyoncé concert. A new AXS verification system slowed purchases by around 40 percent, but that did not stop reps. The company reportedly decided to assign a permanent proxy to each account to reduce the number of blocks. This highly profitable operation ultimately led to a lawsuit filed following a referral from the Federal Trade Commission. However, the defendants have not yet been found legally liable by the court. metadata.title: Concert Tickets Explained: Why They Sell Out in 9 Seconds
metadata.author: Follow The Why
metadata.shortDescription:
Why do concert tickets sell out in 9 seconds?
You refreshed at exactly 10 AM.
Finger on the button.
And the good seats were already gone.

This video follows one arena sale from the inside:
how many tickets never reach the public at all,
how holds and presales carve up the building first,
how bots grab a thousand seats in a minute,
why platinum tickets hit $5,000, what the fees add,
and how the monopoly fight ended in a jury verdict.

Chapters:
00:00 Why do concert tickets sell out in 9 seconds?
00:45 How many tickets never reach the public sale?
01:39 How do presales work — and how many tickets do they take?
03:20 How do bots buy concert tickets?
03:49 What happened in the Taylor Swift Eras Tour sale?
05:42 Why do platinum tickets cost $5,000?
06:43 How much do ticket fees add to the price?
07:14 Does Ticketmaster control ticket sales?
07:42 Did the government sue Live Nation — and who won?

Voice: AI narration.
Music: "Corporate Upbeat" by NastelBom (Pixabay).
Stock: Pexels creators, credited in the video credits file.

Sources: New York Attorney General, "Obstructed View: What's Blocking New Yorkers from Getting Tickets" (Jan 2016): on average 54% of tickets to major events never reach the general public sale (16% insider holds, 38% presales; presales up to 70% at some top shows); one broker's bots bought 1,012 U2 tickets at Madison Square Garden in the first minute despite a 4-ticket limit; brokers resold at an average of 49% above face value. Ticketmaster / Live Nation statements on the Eras Tour presale (Nov 15, 2022): 3.5M+ Verified Fan registrations, 3.5 billion system requests in one day (4x the previous peak), 2M+ tickets sold that day, and the general public sale cancelled for lack of inventory. BOTS Act of 2016; first FTC cases in 2021. U.S. Government Accountability Office (2018): ticket fees averaged 27% on top of face value (range 13–58%); the FTC's 2025 rule now requires the total price up front. Ticketmaster on the Springsteen 2023 onsales: some platinum tickets reached ~$5,000, platinum was ~11% of tickets, average price $262. Oasis reunion onsale (2024): standing tickets listed around £135 were dynamically priced over £350 by checkout; UK competition watchdog investigated. U.S. Department of Justice v. Live Nation (filed May 2024): Ticketmaster handles roughly 80% of primary ticketing at major concert venues; in 2026 a federal jury found Live Nation/Ticketmaster illegally maintained their monopoly and that fans were overcharged $1.72 per ticket; the DOJ separately settled for $280M with service fees capped at 15% at Live Nation amphitheaters. The ~20,000-seat onsale-morning picture is an illustrative framing built from the Attorney General's percentages.

Education only — this video explains how concert ticket sales work. It is not legal or financial advice.
