metadata.title: The BOTS Act: Why Ticket Reselling Communities Live In A Legal Grey Zone
metadata.author: Hustle Audit
metadata.shortDescription: Today lets investigate the Better Online Ticket Sales Act of 2016 and what it actually makes illegal, versus what it leaves wide open. Using the law's own text (S.3183, signed December 2016), the FTC's first-ever enforcement sweep in January 2021 (three brokers, 150,000+ tickets, a $31M judgment cut to $3.7M), and the 2025 escalation against Key Investment Group over Taylor Swift Eras Tour tickets, we map the grey zone that paid ticket-reselling communities operate inside. Sources include congress.gov, ftc.gov, and contemporaneous coverage from Variety and CNN.

segments.text: There is a law that supposedly governs
ticket reselling.
It has been on the books for nearly a
decade.
And yet paid communities that teach
people to buy and flip tickets keep
operating in plain sight, charging
monthly fees, advertising the income,
almost never getting touched.
That is not an accident. It is the
direct result of what the law actually
says, what it pointedly does not say,
and how rarely anyone has bothered to
enforce it. So, we pulled the statute,
the enforcement record, and the recent
crackdown and read it back to front.
This is an audit of the BOTS Act and the
gray zone it leaves behind. Start with
the text, because the text is narrower
than the name suggests.
The Better Online Ticket Sales Act,
signed into federal law in December of
2016, does exactly two things. First, it
makes it illegal to circumvent a
security measure, an access control
system, or any technological control a
ticket seller uses to enforce posted
purchase limits for any public event
with a capacity above 200 people.
In plain terms, that means deploying
bots or buying under fake identities at
scale to blow past the four or six
ticket limit a site has set. Second, it
bans reselling a ticket you obtained
that way if you participated in the
circumvention, could control it, or
should have known about it. That is the
entire prohibition.
The law is not aimed at scalpers as a
class.
It is aimed at one tool, the automated
software that defeats a purchase limit.
The part that matters for anyone
evaluating a paid reselling community,
what the law does not touch. It does not
ban reselling tickets. It does not ban
buying a ticket and flipping it for a
profit. It does not ban buying many
tickets as long as you did it the way
the site allows, by hand within the
posted limit, and it does not, by
itself, cap the resale price. Reselling
above face value is legal across most of
the United States. Only around 15 states
regulated at at
and the rules vary wildly.
New York caps a markup near 10% over
face. California requires a license to
sell above face, and the rest mostly
leave price alone.
So, the federal law targets the bot, and
the bot only.
Manual buying and reselling,
the thing most of these communities
actually teach,
sits in a wide gray zone no federal
statute clearly forbids. Law is only as
real as its enforcement, and here the
record is stark. The BOTS Act was signed
in late 2016 and handed to the Federal
Trade Commission.
The commission then brought zero cases
for more than 4 years.
Not a single action until January of
2021. For the entire stretch when
bot-driven scalping was at its loudest,
when fans could not get near a major on
sale,
the agency holding the only federal tool
used it exactly never.
The penalty on paper was real.
Violations are treated as unfair or
deceptive acts under the FTC Act,
carrying a civil penalty that started
around $16,000 per violation, and with
inflation adjustments, now sits above
But, a serious number that goes
unenforced is just a suggestion.
For 4 years, the BOTS Act was a sign on
an empty road. Enforcement finally
arrived, it arrived narrow.
In January of 2021, the FTC brought its
first ever BOTS Act cases against three
New York ticket brokers.
The allegation was textbook.
They had used bots and other technical
tricks to grab more than 150,000 tickets
to popular events the moment they went
on sale, then resold that inventory for
millions.
The combined civil penalty judgment came
to more than $31 million dollars.
And here is the detail that tells you
how this law really works.
Because the brokers claimed they could
not pay, the court suspended most of it.
They actually paid about $3.7 million
dollars total across all three
operations. So, the very first time the
government used this law, the headline
was $31 million and the real collection
of fraction of it. One sweep, three
defendants, and that was the entire
enforcement history for years. Step back
in the timeline reveals the shape of the
problem.
The law passes in 2016 with bipartisan
support and real intent. Enforcement
does not begin until 2021.
Then, recognizing the gap, lawmakers try
to strengthen the regime. The Ticket Act
clears the House in 2024 aiming at fee
transparency and resale rules, and
senators introduce updates to give the
FTC sharper tools against bots. In March
of 2025, an executive order directs the
commission to, in its words, "rigorously
enforce the BOTS Act" alongside state
attorneys general.
The arc is unmistakable.
A law written, then ignored, then
belatedly tested, then politically
rediscovered nearly a decade later.
The gray zone these communities live in
was not designed. It was carved by the
silence between passing a law and using
it. And the silence may finally be
ending, which changes the math for
anyone buying into a flipping community
right now. In August of 2025, the FTC
sued a Maryland broker operation, Key
Investment Group, doing business under
names like Epic Seats. The allegation
Best used illegal tactics to work around
Ticketmaster's limits and obtain nearly
380,000 tickets between late 2022 and
the end of 2023.
It spent about $57 million buying them
and resold them for roughly $64 million.
For a single Taylor Swift Eras Tour
show, the FTC says it used 49 separate
accounts to buy 273 tickets
against a posted limit of six per
person.
The defense is revealing. The company
argues it used no automated software at
all, no bots, and so did not violate the
act. Whether 49 accounts and 273 tickets
counts as circumvention without a bot is
now the question a court will decide.
And the answer will define how wide the
gray zone really is. So, here is where
it lands for someone weighing a paid
ticket reselling community.
First, the legal reality is sharper than
the marketing admits.
Reselling tickets, even at a markup, is
legal in most of the country. But, the
moment a method depends on defeating a
purchase limit, bots, automated checkout
scripts, or armies of fake accounts
grabbing inventory the platform tried to
cap, you have crossed from the gray zone
into the one thing the BOTS Act was
built to punish with civil penalties now
exceeding $53,000 per violation.
Second, what these communities are
really selling is the gap between those
two states. They teach speed and scale,
and they survive on the enforcement
drought that made the line feel
theoretical.
Third, that drought is visibly ending.
Two enforcement waves in 5 years, an
executive order demanding more, and a
live court fight over whether dozens of
accounts count as circumvention without
a bot.
The question before you pay isn't
whether reselling is legal. It broadly
is.
It's whether the method they teach
depends on beating a limit the seller
set. If it does, the law already has a
name for it, and the gap that protected
it is closing.
Audit closed.

So, we pulled the statute, the enforcement record, and the recent crackdown and read it back to front. This is an audit of the BOTS Act and the gray zone it leaves behind. Start with the text, because the text is narrower than the name suggests. The Better Online Ticket Sales Act, signed into federal law in December of 2016, does exactly two things. First, it makes it illegal to circumvent a security measure, an access control system, or any technological control a ticket seller uses to enforce posted purchase limits for any public event with a capacity above 200 people. In plain terms, that means deploying bots or buying under fake identities at scale to blow past the four or six ticket limit a site has set. Second, it bans reselling a ticket you obtained that way if you participated in the circumvention, could control it, or should have known about it. That is the entire prohibition. The law is not aimed at scalpers as a class. It is aimed at one tool, the automated software that defeats a purchase limit. The part that matters for anyone evaluating a paid reselling community, what the law does not touch. It does not ban reselling tickets. It does not ban buying a ticket and flipping it for a profit. It does not ban buying many tickets as long as you did it the way the site allows, by hand within the posted limit, and it does not, by itself, cap the resale price. Reselling above face value is legal across most of the United States. Only around 15 states regulated at at and the rules vary wildly. New York caps a markup near 10% over face. California requires a license to sell above face, and the rest mostly leave price alone. So, the federal law targets the bot, and the bot only. Manual buying and reselling, the thing most of these communities actually teach, sits in a wide gray zone no federal statute clearly forbids. Law is only as real as its enforcement, and here the record is stark. The BOTS Act was signed in late 2016 and handed to the Federal Trade Commission. The commission then brought zero cases for more than 4 years. Not a single action until January of 2021. For the entire stretch when bot-driven scalping was at its loudest, when fans could not get near a major on sale, the agency holding the only federal tool used it exactly never. The penalty on paper was real. Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act, carrying a civil penalty that started around $16,000 per violation, and with inflation adjustments, now sits above $53,000 each. But, a serious number that goes unenforced is just a suggestion. For 4 years, the BOTS Act was a sign on an empty road. Enforcement finally arrived, it arrived narrow. In January of 2021, the FTC brought its first ever BOTS Act cases against three New York ticket brokers. The allegation was textbook. They had used bots and other technical tricks to grab more than 150,000 tickets to popular events the moment they went on sale, then resold that inventory for millions. The combined civil penalty judgment came to more than $31 million dollars. And here is the detail that tells you how this law really works. Because the brokers claimed they could not pay, the court suspended most of it. They actually paid about $3.7 million dollars total across all three operations. So, the very first time the government used this law, the headline was $31 million and the real collection of fraction of it. One sweep, three defendants, and that was the entire enforcement history for years. Step back in the timeline reveals the shape of the problem. The law passes in 2016 with bipartisan support and real intent. Enforcement does not begin until 2021. Then, recognizing the gap, lawmakers try to strengthen the regime. The Ticket Act clears the House in 2024 aiming at fee transparency and resale rules, and senators introduce updates to give the FTC sharper tools against bots. In March of 2025, an executive order directs the commission to, in its words, "rigorously enforce the BOTS Act" alongside state attorneys general. The arc is unmistakable. A law written, then ignored, then belatedly tested, then politically rediscovered nearly a decade later. The gray zone these communities live in was not designed. It was carved by the silence between passing a law and using it. And the silence may finally be ending, which changes the math for anyone buying into a flipping community right now. In August of 2025, the FTC sued a Maryland broker operation, Key Investment Group, doing business under names like Epic Seats. The allegation Best used illegal tactics to work around Ticketmaster's limits and obtain nearly 380,000 tickets between late 2022 and the end of 2023. It spent about $57 million buying them and resold them for roughly $64 million. For a single Taylor Swift Eras Tour show, the FTC says it used 49 separate accounts to buy 273 tickets against a posted limit of six per person. The defense is revealing. The company argues it used no automated software at all, no bots, and so did not violate the act. Whether 49 accounts and 273 tickets counts as circumvention without a bot is now the question a court will decide. And the answer will define how wide the gray zone really is. So, here is where it lands for someone weighing a paid ticket reselling community. First, the legal reality is sharper than the marketing admits. Reselling tickets, even at a markup, is legal in most of the country. But, the moment a method depends on defeating a purchase limit, bots, automated checkout scripts, or armies of fake accounts grabbing inventory the platform tried to cap, you have crossed from the gray zone into the one thing the BOTS Act was built to punish with civil penalties now exceeding $53,000 per violation. Second, what these communities are really selling is the gap between those two states. They teach speed and scale, and they survive on the enforcement drought that made the line feel theoretical. Third, that drought is visibly ending. Two enforcement waves in 5 years, an executive order demanding more, and a live court fight over whether dozens of accounts count as circumvention without a bot. The question before you pay isn't whether reselling is legal. It broadly is. It's whether the method they teach depends on beating a limit the seller set. If it does, the law already has a name for it, and the gap that protected it is closing. Audit closed.

metadata.title: Limit 8 Per Customer… 1,300 Accounts? The DOJ's BOTS Act Case Against REPS, Explained
metadata.author: Dot Detective
metadata.shortDescription:
The ticket limit said 8. The government says one broker showed up as 1,300 "customers" for a single concert.

On Oct 15, 2026, the Justice Department, on a referral from the FTC, sued San Diego ticket broker REPS & Company and three of its executives under the BOTS Act and the FTC Act. The complaint alleges REPS used thousands of ticket accounts in employees' and partners' names, virtual credit cards, proxy IPs, VPNs and multi-session browsers to get around purchase limits, spending more than $1.3 billion on over 18.5 million tickets and making at least $120.8 million in profit.

REPS denies the allegations. Its president told TicketNews: "As the lawsuit admits, we use real people, using real accounts, to purchase tickets. We never use bots."

Everything in this video is an allegation. No court has ruled, and there has been no finding of liability. Docket status is as of Oct 21, 2026.

1:09 How it allegedly worked

- DOJ press release (Oct 15, 2026): https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-files-complaint-against-california-ticket-broker-using-unlawful-tactics
- FTC press release (Oct 15, 2026): https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-sues-ticket-broker-over-unlawful-tactics-used-buy-millions-tickets-popular-live-events

president

and that the FTC's theory would destroy
the secondary ticket market and hurt
consumers. "More importantly, it is not
the law. We look forward to presenting
our case in court." And that's the real
fight here. The government says the law
covers more than software bots. It
covers getting around the limits,
however you do it. Reps says real humans
with real accounts aren't what the law
targets. That question of what counts as

matter a lot beyond this one company.

Department can't fix. We'll keep

metadata.title: Ticketmaster Fees Hit 44%. The FTC Is Suing. I Read the Fine Print.
metadata.author: The Fine Print Audit
metadata.shortDescription:
The FTC alleges Ticketmaster collected $16.4 billion in mandatory fees up to 44% of the ticket price between 2019 and 2024. Since May 12, 2025, a federal rule requires the first concert ticket price you see to be the total price—so I audited the rule, the complaint, and Ticketmaster's own fee definitions.

What was audited (read and recorded as of October 16, 2026):
- FTC Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees (16 CFR Part 464, effective May 12, 2025) and official FTC FAQ guidance on "convenience fees," "service fees," and "processing fees" (https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/rule-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-frequently-asked-questions)
- Ticketmaster Help Center: "How are ticket prices and fees determined" (https://help.ticketmaster.com/hc/en-us/articles/9663528775313-How-are-ticket-prices-and-fees-determined) & "What is the All-In Price" (https://help.ticketmaster.com/hc/en-us/articles/35127799858193-What-is-the-All-In-Price), defining the Service Fee, Facility Charge, Delivery Fee, and Resale Service Fee
- FTC and 7 states' lawsuit against Live Nation and Ticketmaster filed Sept 18, 2025 (Live Nation is contesting the allegations in court; motion to dismiss denied Sept 28, 2026)
- DOJ antitrust settlement status, 22-state jury verdict, and the April 2026 StubHub $10M FTC refund order
- Real resale spread example reported Oct 7, 2026 ($299 listed Bruno Mars seat, $422.45 buyer total, $254.15 seller payout after a $44.85 / 15% seller fee)
- State all-in pricing statutes: California Civ. Code 1770(a)(29), New York Arts & Cultural Affairs Law 25.07(4), and Minnesota Stat. 325D.44

metadata.title: Decibel and Docket covers hearing on AB1720, California concert ticket resale price cap.
metadata.author: Decibel & Docket
metadata.shortDescription: Dave Brooks with Decibel and Docket streams a recent Consumer Privacy Committee hearing of the California Assembly examinng the impact of AB1720, a bill that would cap markup on concert tickets at 10 percent plus face value. The hearing examines a bill brought by Assemblyman Matt Haney and includes testimony from Randy Nichols and Joe Rinaldi, as well as representatives from Stubhub. The testimony follows the recent SDNY jury decision in the Ticketmaster and Live Nation antitrust case.

metadata.title: Why Concert Tickets Are So Expensive (Who Really Gets Your Money)
metadata.author: Hidden Price
metadata.shortDescription:
Why are concert tickets so expensive? In a U.S. GAO review of a sample of events, fees added an average of 27% to the price of tickets from primary sellers and 31% on resale sites — and some look-alike resale sites charged more than 40%.

In this episode we follow the money: who sets the fee and who keeps it, where the face value goes, why so few tickets ever reach the public at face value, how bots and resellers capture the gap, what dynamic and tiered pricing actually do, and what happened when the Justice Department and the states took Live Nation and Ticketmaster to court.

Chapters
0:00 Fees: 27%, 31%, 40%+
0:41 Where the fee goes
1:46 Where the ticket price goes
2:31 Why you can't get face value
3:58 Dynamic pricing
4:56 One company in the middle
7:16 What changed
7:52 What this means for you
8:33 Next episode

Sources
- U.S. Government Accountability Office, "Event Ticket Sales: Market Characteristics and Consumer Protection Issues" (GAO-18-347), April 2018 — fee averages come from a nongeneralizable sample of events
- New York State Attorney General, "Obstructed View: What's Blocking New Yorkers from Getting Tickets," 2016 (fees averaging 21% of face value; $42 fee example; 46% / 38% / 16% ticket allocation for top shows, 2012–2015; 1,012 tickets bought in one minute; six brokers' average markup of 49%)
- Live Nation Entertainment, Form 10-K for fiscal 2025 (SEC): ticketing revenue $3.1B, 346M fee-bearing tickets, $37.1B fee-bearing gross transaction value, 29.2% ticketing operating margin; concerts revenue $20.9B (83% of total), 0.4% concerts operating margin; "our artists receive the majority of all ticketing revenue"; venues "set the ticketing service fee" and "typically retain the majority of these fees"; resale companies paid by both seller and buyer; 805M fans, 460 venues
- Live Nation Entertainment, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 (SEC): May 2024 Justice Department complaint and remedies sought; March 2026 settlement ($280M fund, subject to court approval); April 15, 2026 jury verdict for the litigating states; the company's plan to appeal and $450M estimated loss; September 2025 FTC complaint (allegations) and motion to dismiss
- NBC News, April 15, 2026 ($1.72 per-ticket overcharge at major concert venues; the states' 86% share claim and Live Nation's ~44% figure; Live Nation's statement that the award covers tickets at 257 venues, about 20% of its total)
- U.S. Department of Justice, December 2019 release on the 2010 Live Nation–Ticketmaster consent decree
- UK Competition and Markets Authority, Ticketmaster consumer protection case (investigation opened Sept. 5, 2024; undertakings signed Sept. 15, 2025); CMA statement that it had not found evidence of dynamic pricing in the Oasis on-sale, as reported by Music Business Worldwide and RPC
- Ticketmaster's position on dynamic pricing, as reported by Complete Music Update and Music Week
- FTC Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees (16 C.F.R. Part 464), effective May 12, 2025
- FTC press release, April 9, 2026: StubHub settlement ($10M; the FTC's allegations, settled)
The "about 8 cents per dollar" and margin comparisons are our own calculations from Live Nation's reported figures. Lawsuit claims are described as allegations unless a jury or court found them. Remedies in the states' case had not been decided as of Live Nation's latest quarterly report.

metadata.title: Beyoncé fans complain of inconsistent ticket prices for Cowboy Carter Tour
metadata.author: CBS News
metadata.shortDescription:
Some Beyoncé fans say they're seeing inconsistent ticket prices for the Cowboy Carter Tour, with some social media users pointing to seats in the same section going for different prices depending on when you bought the tickets. In a statement to CBS News, Ticketmaster said, "Prices were set in advance of the sales by the tour. Ticketmaster does not have surge pricing or dynamic algorithms to adjust ticket prices." Andrew Mall, associate professor of music at Northeastern University, joined CBS News to discuss the issue.

Beyonce's Cowboy Carter Tour Struggles to Sell Out Stadiums | Firstpost America | N18G

Beyonce's highly anticipated Cowboy Carter Tour is facing unexpectedly slow ticket sales, despite initial demand crashing Ticketmaster when tickets were first released in February. With less than two weeks to go before the opening show on April 28 at Los Angeles' SoFi Stadium, more than 3,200 seats remain unsold, with resale tickets listed for as low as $35. Subsequent LA shows also have over 3,800 tickets still available each. The trend continues nationwide, with over 5,500 tickets available for the final New Jersey date and more than 5,800 in Atlanta, including 50% of floor seats. Despite this, Live Nation maintains that 94% of tickets have been sold.

metadata.title: Taylor Swift’s ‘Eras Tour’ Tickets Crash Ticketmaster
metadata.author: Inside Edition
metadata.shortDescription: Ticketmaster crashes as millions of Taylor Swift fans try to buy tickets to her world tour. A mother and daughter found themselves next in line in the virtual queue until they were suddenly behind 2,000 other people. Adding to the chaos, some tickets were reselling for $45,000. Ticketmaster issued this statement: “there has been historically unprecedented demand with millions showing up” to buy tickets for Swift’s tour, which caused “intermittent issues.”

segments.text: Dynamic ticket pricing is a strategy
that has become increasingly popular in
various industries, especially sports,
entertainment, and travel. But what
exactly does it entail? Well, instead of
having static prices, dynamic pricing
allows ticket prices to fluctuate based
on demand, time, and other variables.
Now, let's delve into the details.
Starting with the pros, dynamic pricing
can maximize revenue for sellers. By
adjusting prices to match real-time
demand, organizations can ensure they're
getting the most value out of each
ticket. For example, a popular concert
might see ticket prices rise as the
venue fills up, reflecting the high
demand. This approach can help sellers
make more informed pricing decisions
based on data trends and market
conditions. Another advantage is
improved inventory management.

metadata.title: TICKETMASTER REFUND POLICY UPDATE FOR CANCELLED AND POSTPONED EVENTS | TICKET REFUND PLAN
metadata.author: thumbsuprun
metadata.shortDescription:
Ticketmaster has made many changes to their ticket refund policy over the last month, and as a result I wanted to talk about how you can actually request a refund for your tickets!

Ticketmaster had made a change in late March/early April 2020 to their ticket refund policy, removing the ability to request a refund for postponed events, and only allowing refunds for events which have been officially cancelled. Previously, any events which were rescheduled, postponed, or cancelled were all eligible for a refund (with a couple of exceptions). This change was done very quietly and was picked up by the media on April 10, 2020, and it quickly spread across Twitter.

By April 14, 2020 Ticketmaster had to issue a response to the dramatic outcry from fans looking for refunds, and on April 17, 2020 they actually ended up capitulating and having to implement a new type of refund policy. They initially introduced the new refund policy as the "Rock When You're Ready' program, whereby cancelled events were able to get refunded like before, or you could request a credit for your tickets instead at a rate of up to 150%. For postponed events which had a new rescheduled date, these tickets would also be eligible for a refund or the 150% credit, and both types of tickets would be able to make their selections for one month beginning May 1 to May 30. 

There were still issues with this program though as events which were postponed without a rescheduled date would not qualify for this program. By April 24, 2020, Ticketmaster released an update to their policy, firstly renaming it the "Ticket Refund Plan", and also adding in another section which stated that any events which were postponed with NO rescheduled date within 60 days would also be eligible for a refund or credit option. 

Ticketmaster is having cash-flow issues with the numerous amount of ticket refunds that are to be requested, so this new policy will allow for them to manage their cash-flow much better, though it will still be difficult to issue out all refunds in a timely manner. As a result, Ticketmaster is giving itself 30 days to process these refund requests.

To be able to request the refund, beginning May 1, 2020 you will be able to log into your Ticketmaster account and begin making your selections for any eligible events. Be sure to complete your selection process before the May 30 deadline passes though or else you may end up not being able to request a refund later on.

metadata.title: Players, coaches continue to resell Super Bowl tickets, despite ban on the practice
metadata.author: 24H SPORT
metadata.shortDescription:
Players, coaches continue to resell Super Bowl tickets, despite ban on the practice.
MINNEAPOLIS — About one-third of Super Bowl tickets go to the 30 NFL teams not playing in the game. NFL rules state that those tickets are not to be sold for a profit on the secondary market, but that’s where some can be found as the New England Patriots and Philadelphia Eagles prepare to meet in Super Bowl LII on Sunday, according to ticket brokers

One broker told USA TODAY Sports that about 80% of the tickets he’s had up for sale this week — with prices starting at $3,500 apiece — came directly from players and coaches and from their agents. The broker was granted anonymity because the practice of selling those tickets is banned by the NFL. 

Players can purchase two tickets under terms of the collective bargaining agreement, which states the tickets are “subject to reasonable safeguards to avoid scalping of the tickets.” That doesn’t count the bigger allotment that goes to the teams involved in the Super Bowl.

“NFL personnel cannot resell above face value,” NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy said in a statement to USA TODAY Sports.

metadata.title: Why the World's Biggest Stars Accept $0 for the Super Bowl
metadata.author: Apparently Athletic
metadata.shortDescription:
Do Super Bowl halftime performers get paid? "There is not an appearance fee," the NFL says. So why do the biggest stars on Earth say yes, and who's really getting paid?
We follow the paycheck, the deal and the price: union scale, Michael Jackson's yes in 1993, the ads and the name on the show, and Jay-Z, named the headliner for February 14, 2027.

In 2025, 133.5 million people watched the halftime show, more than the game itself, according to the NFL. Kendrick Lamar reportedly got union scale: about $1,000 a day. And in 2021, Billboard reported that The Weeknd was spending $7 million of his own money on his show.

CHAPTERS
0:00 "There is not an appearance fee"
0:49 The paycheck: union scale
1:39 The deal: Michael Jackson, 1993
2:53 The price of twelve minutes
4:12 The money runs the other way
5:21 What the stars get back, and Jay-Z

A note on the numbers: the NFL doesn't publish its contracts or the cost of the show. Figures on pay, production, ad prices and the Apple Music deal come from press reports and are presented as such.

CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0): Toni Salabasev, Brian Ziff
Press images and logos are credited on screen and belong to their owners.

metadata.title: Super Bowl I vs Today: No Sellout at $12. Now Seats Start at $950
metadata.author: Overtime Economics
metadata.shortDescription:
The first Super Bowl, on January 15, 1967, left over 30,000 seats unsold at 6 to 12 dollars, and a 30-second commercial cost about 42,000 dollars. Sixty years later, Disney's Super Bowl LXI telecast on ESPN and ABC sold out with 30-second spots that reportedly went for 8 to 9 million dollars, and resale seats already list above 5,000 dollars before anyone knows who is playing.

Every Super Bowl price, 60 years apart, in today's dollars (BLS consumer price index, September 2026): tickets and resale prices, the 30-second ad, the TV audience, the halftime show, the stadiums (the 1923 Los Angeles Coliseum and SoFi Stadium) and the winners' share, which the players' union contract sets at 188,000 dollars for Super Bowl LXI. The 950-dollar face value is last February's cheapest seat at Super Bowl LX; the NFL has not published LXI face values yet. Resale figures are TicketIQ's game-day listings for LX and TickPick's LXI listings on November 9, 2026. Ad prices and production costs are as reported. Images are illustrative. No real people or places are shown.

0:25 The Twelve-Dollar Seat
2:23 Thirty Seconds
4:24 Halftime
5:03 The Building
6:15 The Winners' Check
8:07 Who Got Richer

segments.text: What happens when a Super Bowl can't sell out at 12 dollars?
At the very first one, over 30,000 seats went unsold.
Last February, the cheapest face-value seat cost 950 dollars.
A 42,000-dollar commercial now sells for about 8 million.
Adjust for sixty years of inflation, and one price barely moved.
So which one, and who got richer instead?
We'll put every 1967 price into today's dollars,
using the government's inflation index.
Start in Los Angeles, on a Sunday afternoon in January 1967.
The game wasn't even officially called the Super Bowl yet.
It was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game: Green Bay against Kansas City.
They came from rival leagues that had agreed to merge in 1966.
The best seat in the house cost 12 dollars.
The cheapest went for just six dollars, and fans still stayed away.
The stadium held about 94,000 people. Only 61,946 came through the gates.
If you lived nearby, you couldn't even watch it on TV.
Los Angeles was blacked out, so locals needed a ticket to watch.
Green Bay won, 35 to 10, in front of all those empty seats.
In today's money, that best seat would cost about 123 dollars.
Super Bowl one's cheapest seat, in today's money: about 61 dollars. Last February's:
That's about 15 times as much after inflation, and most fans never see that price.
Face-value prices alone rose 136 percent in ten years,
Sports Business Journal found.
And face-value seats aren't sold to the public.
They go through teams and the league.
Each team had to offer at least 4,350 seats to its season-ticket holders.
For most fans, that means resale. On game day, listings averaged about 8,100.
Even the cheapest resale ticket was listed at about 4,950.
Would you pay 950 dollars for the worst seat, or watch from your couch?
The couch, by the way, is the one seat that's still free.
Hold that answer. The ticket isn't even the price that grew the most.
How much did thirty seconds of Super Bowl one cost an advertiser?
Take a guess. The real number sounds like a typo.
About 42,000 dollars, on either network. Now run it through inflation.
That's about 430,000 in today's money. This February: about 8 million.
And that's for the exact same thirty seconds of airtime.
At that price, every second on screen costs about 267,000 dollars.
In 1967, the same second cost about 1,400 dollars.
Before inflation, that's about 190 times more per second.
Back then, rival networks CBS and NBC both carried the game, side by side.
It remains the only Super Bowl ever carried by two rival networks.
Super Bowl one drew 51.18 million viewers. Last February's drew 125.6 million.
Even per viewer, after inflation, an ad now costs about seven and a half times more.
The audience grew, but the price of reaching it grew much faster.
Like seeing the bill behind the show? Subscribe, and get a new one every day.
Last February's game was the most-watched show in NBC's history.
NBC had sold out its ads by early September,
the earliest sellout confirmed until then.
A handful of its spots reportedly went for more than 10 million.
This February belongs to ESPN and ABC, ESPN's first Super Bowl ever.
Disney reportedly asked 10 million a spot,
plus a matching buy on its other channels.
Advertisers balked. Spots reportedly went for 8 to 9 million,
and sold out by early August.
And the NFL's TV deals reportedly bring in about 10 billion dollars a year.
So networks charge advertisers more.
But halftime hides the strangest bargain of all.
Super Bowl one's halftime had 300 pigeons and 10,000 balloons.
The stars were two college marching bands and a jazz trumpeter.
A high school drill team from nearby Anaheim performed too.
And a ticket to see all of it topped out at 12 dollars.
Today's headliner is paid union scale, about 1,000 dollars a day, reports say.
The league covers the production. For the 2020 show, that was reportedly 13 million.
So the biggest act of the night works for scale, on a stage worth millions.
For the artist, the payment is the audience: well over 100 million people.
And the building they play in grew even faster than the ad.
Super Bowl one was played in a stadium built for under a million dollars.
The Los Angeles Coliseum, finished in 1923, cost about 955,000 dollars.
Super Bowl sixty-one will be played at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, nearby.
It opened in 2020. Its first estimate was 2.66 billion dollars.
By the end, it was privately built for an estimated 5.5 billion.
It seats about 70,000 fans, with room to expand for the biggest events.
The Coliseum, in today's money: about 19 million. SoFi: about 5.5 billion.
That's nearly 300 times as much, even after inflation.
It already hosted Super Bowl fifty-six in 2022, when the Rams won at home.
Last February, 70,823 people filled Levi's Stadium for Super Bowl sixty.
A smaller stadium than in 1967, and a bigger crowd anyway.
The crowd grew a little. The money it brings in grew a lot.
So tickets, ads and buildings all exploded. Now the one price that didn't.
Super Bowl one paid each winning Packer 15,000 dollars.
Each player on the losing Chiefs got 7,500 dollars.
In 1968, the players' first union deal set a veteran's minimum salary at 10,000.
So one game paid one and a half times a veteran's minimum for a season.
Today the bonus is written into the players' union contract, year by year.
Every playoff round has its own check, set years in advance.
Win every playoff round, and the total comes to about 400,000.
The amount is the same for the star quarterback and the last backup.
Super Bowl sixty-one's winners get 188,000 each,
over twelve times the first Super Bowl's bonus.
Each player on the losing side still gets 113,000 dollars.
Now adjust both of those for inflation, the way we did for everything else.
1967's 15,000 is about 153,600 in today's money. This February: 188,000.
Sixty years later, the winners' real raise is about 22 percent.
The losing side did a little better: about 47 percent above inflation.
That's the one price that barely moved in sixty years.
And the contract lifts it just 10,000 a year, through the 2030 season.
But here's the twist: the players didn't get poorer. Their money moved elsewhere.
This season, the minimum salary for a rookie is 885,000 dollars.
So the winner's bonus is now about a fifth of a rookie's minimum.
Back then, one game paid more than a veteran's minimum salary.
Now it's a nice bonus.
So, sixty years apart, who really got richer from the Super Bowl?
After inflation: the ad, about 19 times. Cheapest seat, 15. Audience, 2.5.
Winner's bonus, 1.2.
Fans pay more for the seat. Advertisers pay more for the screen.
The game itself is still sixty minutes of football.
Everything around it got pricier.
If Super Bowl bonuses had grown like the ads,
each winner would get about 2.9 million.
The Super Bowl now sells one night four ways.
Seats, thirty-second slots, a halftime stage, and a five-billion-dollar building.
The players' money moved into salaries, not into the bonus for winning it.
Super Bowl 61 has no teams yet, and resale seats already start above 5,000 dollars.
It's played a short drive from where twelve-dollar seats once went unsold.
Would you pay 950 dollars for the worst seat, or stay on your couch?
Tomorrow at noon: Neymar to PSG, a 222-million-euro record still standing,
and what it bought.

metadata.title: Business Meals and Entertainment Tax deduction - What You Should Know
metadata.author: David Fiene
metadata.shortDescription:
The IRS states that client and prospect business meals can be deducted, which was limited to 50% prior to 2021 but In 2021 and 2022, this deduction is 100%

But, there are several rules that you should be aware of in regards to what is and isn’t deductible and what proof you need to substantiate the deduction..

So in this video, I’m going to walk you through those rules including what you should keep to support this deduction. 

Chapters
00:00 Introduction
00:47 Basic Rule
01:44 Ordinary and Necessary
02:46 Lavish or Extravagant
03:27 Presence
05:28 Documentation
06:17 Key Takeaways

metadata.title: HOW DYNAMIC TICKET PRICING & OFFICIAL PLATINUM SEATS WORK ON TICKETMASTER
metadata.author: thumbsuprun
metadata.shortDescription:
Time to learn all about how dynamic ticket pricing and official platinum seats work on Ticketmaster! I dive into how dynamic ticket pricing has evolved over time, and the eventual rise of the official platinum seat. Ticketmaster has been using a dynamic ticket pricing system for many years now, just like many other industries. By being able to raise (or lower) ticket prices, they are able to maximize the amount of revenue generated year after year.

Their official platinum seating program on the other hand is simply designed to match the expected market values of seating in potentially prime locations. However, some of the seating options set aside for official platinum seating have left more questions than answers, especially when they are located in side view and near the back of the venue as well.

Lastly, with dynamic ticket pricing, there have been many issues with its implementation, especially with events that saw ticket prices change between the time they were added to the cart and when they appeared in the checkout process. I have an article from CBC which dives into what happened with a Rolling Stones concert in 2019 that went on sale, and I think it's just another reason which proves being patient is key in your ticket buying process.

Thank you Helix Sleep for sponsoring! Visit https://helixsleep.com/scottcramer to take advantage of their President's Day Sale exclusive partner offer and get 27% Off Sitewide! 

Ticketmaster has been in hot water with artists and fans since before I was even born. They tack insane fees onto every ticket you purchase on their site, their business model incentivises bots to buy up loads of tickets and resell them to fans who will overpay, and they have seemingly monopolized the industry past the point of return. Fun! Let’s talk about it. Enjoy. 

There were a lot of segments that I had to cut out of this video for the sake of time, and those are available on my Patreon! https://patreon.com/ScottsTOL

metadata.title: s-ticket for staff: box office, parking, refunds and door check-in (5-minute guide)
metadata.author: Brian Jones
metadata.shortDescription:
A quick guide for box office and front-of-house staff using s-ticket:
selling tickets with seat-by-seat prices, complimentary tickets and parking, blocking house seats,
changing prices and giving refunds, and checking people in at the door with a phone.

The venues and customers shown are fictional, created to demonstrate the system.

segments.text: Welcome to s-ticket. This short video shows staff everything they need for a show:
selling tickets and parking at the box office, changing prices and giving refunds,
and checking people in at the door.
To get started, open the staff entry page. There's no username or password.
Just answer the little sum, which keeps out robots.
This is the admin home page. From here you can reach the box office, performances,
bookings, members, and door check-in.
Let's sell some tickets. In the box office, choose the performance. Here,
it's the evening show of Aladdin.
Then choose the section. The seat plan shows every seat, coloured by price band.
Dark seats are already sold.
Orange seats are being chosen by someone booking online right now, so they can't be sold here until they're let go.
Click the seats you want. They turn pink, and appear in the list of tickets below.
Each seat can have its own price: full, member, or concession.
For a complimentary ticket, choose Other price,
then enter an amount (here £0) and a reason, such as a press ticket.
If the customer is driving, tick Add parking and type in the car's registration.
The parking fee is added to the total, and it covers the day of the show,
from arrival until midnight.
Next, the customer's name and phone number.
These are needed for every sale, so we can get in touch if a show is cancelled.
Add their email address if they have one.
Choose whether to print the ticket now, email it, or both. Then click Book & issue ticket.
Done. The booking is confirmed with its receipt number and total,
and the ticket is on its way to the customer.
This is the ticket the customer receives,
with the car's registration printed on it for parking.
The QR code is what gets checked at the door.
You can also take seats off sale online, for example house seats. Switch to Block seats,
give a reason, and click the seats. They turn blue.
Blocked seats can still be sold here at the box office. To put one back on sale online,
just click it again.
For unreserved events, like Jazz in the Cellar, there's no seat plan.
Just enter how many tickets at each price, and the page shows how many are left.
The Bookings page lists everyone booked for a performance, with their contact details.
Here's tonight's show, Blithe Spirit.
At the top are the number of tickets and the takings.
You can download the list as a spreadsheet, copy every email address,
which is handy if a show has to be cancelled, or print it.
To change a booking, click Manage, under its receipt number.
This is the Manage page for a single booking. At the top: the show, the customer,
and what they've paid.
Margaret is a member, but she was charged the full price. Under Change prices,
switch both seats to the member price.
The page works out the difference: here, £6.00 to give back. Say how it was given back,
add a reason, and save.
The change is kept in the booking's history, so the takings always add up.
Parking can be changed here too.
Type in a car's registration and add it, or tick a car to take it off and refund the fee.
The customer is emailed a new ticket, because the registration is printed on it.
Now, a refund. Tom Reeves can't come tonight, so let's open his booking.
Under Refund tickets, tick the seats to refund. The amount fills in by itself,
but you can change it if you need to.
Choose how the money was given back, and add a reason.
Leave the email box ticked, to send Tom a confirmation.
Click the button to cancel the booking. The seats go straight back on sale,
and Tom's old ticket will no longer be accepted at the door.
If you refund only some of the seats,
the customer is emailed a new ticket for the seats they keep.
On the night, door staff use their phone. Open the door check-in page and log in once.
It stays logged in for the evening.
Add your first name, so the list shows who let each person in.
Tap Start camera, and point it at the ticket's QR code.
If the booking includes parking,
the car's registration is shown as well, so the car park can be checked at the same time.
Green means the ticket is valid. James has three seats,
but only two of his party are here. Tap a seat to leave it out, then tap Admit.
When the ticket is scanned again, it shows amber. Two are in,
and the third can be admitted when they arrive.
If a ticket has already been used, or someone shares a screenshot of it, it shows red,
with the time it was used and who let them in.
A refunded ticket shows red too, so it can't be used.
The Door list shows everyone booked, and how many are in. You can search by name,
seat or receipt number.
Someone forgotten their ticket? Find them in the list and tap Admit.
And if you make a mistake, tap Undo.
Every phone on the doors stays in step, because the list updates every few seconds.
And that's it. For more detail,
see the Admin guide and the Customer guide on the s-ticket website. Thanks for watching.

metadata.title: IT Helpdesk Best Practices That Reduce Tickets And Keep Work Moving
metadata.author: NDSE
metadata.shortDescription:
A helpdesk ticket is rarely just an IT glitch—it’s a blocked payroll run, a missed customer call, or an invoice approval brought to a dead stop.

The best helpdesks don't just close tickets; they protect workflows, stop repeat interruptions, and resolve issues before downtime impacts revenue.

In this video, you'll learn:
- How to categorize and triage tickets by true business impact
- Proven helpdesk best practices that achieve sub-15-minute response times and high first-call resolution
- Plain-English communication strategies that keep users confident during outages
- How tracking root-cause patterns eliminates recurring IT tickets for good

Read more: https://ndse.net/it-help-desk-best-practices/ 

Connect with us: 
https://www.ndse.net/ 
https://www.facebook.com/NDSEINC/ 
http://www.youtube.com/@NdseNet 
https://creators.spotify.com/pod/show/ndse 
https://www.linkedin.com/company/network-data-security-experts-inc-/ 
Frank Ernesto, CEO of Network Data Security Experts, Inc. (NDSE)
https://www.linkedin.com/in/fernesto4/   
Michael Pfaff, Director of Operations for Network Data Security Experts, Inc. (NDSE)
https://www.linkedin.com/in/mspfaff/

segments.text: A help desk ticket is rarely just a
ticket. It can be a payroll deadline
blocked by a password reset, an invoice
run delayed by file access, or a
customer call disrupted because [music]
Teams, Slack, Wi-Fi, a printer, or a
scanner stops cooperating.
As Michael Pfaff, director of operations
at Network Data Security Experts Inc.
says,
the best help desk teams do more than
close tickets. [music] They restore the
workflow, document the fix, and watch
for patterns that will interrupt users
again.
That is the real issue. Small IT
interruptions quickly become workflow
problems, security concerns, and
downtime risks. [music] Strong help desk
practices start with visibility.
Every request needs to be logged,
assigned, and documented, [music]
whether it is a password reset or
printer jam issue. Clear notes about the
device, user, [music]
system, and fix help shorten future
troubleshooting.
The next step [music] is smart
categorization and escalation. Access
and password issues, device problems,
network and Wi-Fi connectivity, software
and communication tools, and
cybersecurity concerns should not sit in
one vague queue.
Categories work best when they reflect
how work actually happens. Approvals,
file [music] sharing, customer
communication, billing, supported
devices, covered software, and security
concerns.
Fast resolution also depends on clear
expectations.
Users should know when to expect a
response and what information to
provide. Many issues can be handled
during first contact when technicians
know the environment. Repeat issues
should trigger review, not another
temporary fix.
[music] Remote support can fit many
software and access issues, while
recurring printer, scanner, or
workstation failures may need hands-on
troubleshooting.
Communication matters just as much as
technical skill.
Support should acknowledge the blocked
invoice, customer meeting, or file
deadline, explain next steps in English
and follow up after the fix. Better help
desk practices lead to fewer repeat
issues, smoother onboarding, clearer
budgeting, stronger cybersecurity
awareness, and less disruption across
daily work. To go deeper, read the full

playlist.

metadata.title: Bulk Import Delivery Orders From a Spreadsheet | Zippykind
metadata.author: Zippykind
metadata.shortDescription:
Bulk upload delivery orders from a spreadsheet: follow the Data Importer wizard, map columns, save a template, and import up to 1,000 rows per file.

For businesses that send deliveries through a courier that runs on Zippykind.

Start the 14 day trial: https://zippykind.com/signup?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=training_videos&utm_content=video50

Full training playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLBNw-Yr3TunM

Watch next: Label Packages and Mark Them Ready for Pickup https://youtu.be/i6gX6-bIoVg

CHAPTERS
0:00 Three ways to add tickets
0:12 The Data Importer wizard
0:36 Several items on one ticket
0:57 Data mapping
1:10 Import and coordinates

TRANSCRIPT
There are three ways to get delivery tickets into Zippykind: the Add New Ticket form at the top of every page, an API integration, or the Data Importer. Let's look at the Data Importer. Open the Data Importer and follow the wizard. Zippykind maps your columns for you, so even if your spreadsheet doesn't look the same every time, your data still lands in the right place. You can import deliveries with or without order information, and your customers and products too. If you're the client of a courier, include your Location ID in the file. You'll find it in the Locations Manager. To add several items to one ticket, put each item on its own row under the ticket and leave the first column blank on those rows, like you see here. If the first row of your file holds the column names, tick "The first row of my file is a header row." Then choose your file and continue. Each file can hold up to 1,000 rows. Next comes Data Mapping, where you tell the importer what each column means. Most of them are matched for you already. On the next step, check that everything looks right. Every row is selected, so untick anything you don't want. If your file looks the same every time, save the column mapping as a template and the next file maps itself. Then import. It takes a minute or two for Zippykind to generate the coordinates for your tickets, and before that time, the tickets will be held back from the dashboard map and driver's app. If you see an orange warning symbol in front of the address on the Tickets Manager, coordinates are still waiting to be fetched, or there is an issue with the address you provided. Click the symbol to refetch. And that's getting your orders into Zippykind.

metadata.title: NFL Ticket Prices Explained (How They Became Expensive)
metadata.author: Football Explainer
metadata.shortDescription:
NFL tickets have gotten a lot more expensive, but how did we get here?

In this video, we break down the history of NFL ticket prices and explain the major factors that have changed the cost of watching a game in person. From the early days of the league to the modern NFL, we look at how stadiums, demand, team popularity, premium seating, pricing strategies, and the secondary market have transformed the cost of being an NFL fan.

We’ll also look at why some games can cost dramatically more than others, where your money actually goes when you buy a ticket, and why getting through the stadium gates can feel like the easy part of the expense.

So how did watching an NFL game go from an affordable Sunday activity to a major expense?

Let's find out.

#NFL #Football #NFLHistory

Television contracts had become enormous, national sponsorships had grown, and media money had become the financial foundation of the league. That meant the NFL could survive a season in which millions of fans couldn't attend games. But surviving wasn't the same as replacing the stadium. Teams had invested huge sums into buildings designed to make money from live customers. A luxury suite with nobody inside it doesn't generate luxury suite revenue. A parking lot without cars doesn't sell parking. A concession stand without fans has a very obvious problem. The 2020 season therefore became a bizarre experiment in what the NFL looked like when the most traditional part of its business model was temporarily removed. And fans noticed the absence, too. Spending decades being told that watching football from the stadium was an experience worth paying a premium for. Millions of people suddenly had no choice but to watch from home. The league was forced to prove that the live experience still had value once fans were allowed back. In 2021, the stadiums began filling again. The NFL's average paid attendance jumped to more than 64,000 per game, compared with just 3,922 in 2020. By 2022, it was nearly 66,800, and it remained above 66,000 in both 2023 and 2024. The rebound was remarkably fast. And that brought the ticket back to the center of the story because fans weren't just returning to watch football. They were returning to an NFL that had become even more expensive and technologically sophisticated than the one they had left. The pandemic hadn't erased the ticket economy. It had merely paused it. And when it restarted, the price tag kept moving upward. The ticket is now an experience. When fans returned to NFL stadiums, they came back to a business that had spent decades becoming more sophisticated about what people were willing to pay. The basic ticket was still there, of course, but by this point, there wasn't really one NFL ticket market anymore. There were hundreds of different markets operating inside every stadium. A seat in the upper deck for a bad December matchup could be relatively affordable. A lower level seat for a division rivalry could cost several times as much. A playoff ticket could jump again. A premium club seat could live in an entirely different financial universe. And a Super Bowl ticket was basically its own economic species. The average regular NFL ticket reached $120.94 in 2023, according to Team Marketing Report. That was an 8.6% 6% increase from the previous year's figure. More importantly, TMR's fan cost index, which estimates the cost for a family of four, including tickets, food, drinks, parking, and other typical expenses, reached $63,163. So, if you look only at the ticket, you might think the story is simple. The average price went from a few dollars decades ago to around $121. But that actually understates what happened. The real transformation is the cost of the entire experience. And that's really the final stage of this story. The NFL didn't simply increase ticket prices. It built an increasingly sophisticated system for pricing scarcity. There are only so many seats in a stadium. There are only eight regular season home games under the traditional schedule. There are only so many chances to see your team play a major opponent at home. And if that team happens to be good, the demand can become enormous. The modern ticket market is therefore built around a very different idea from the one that existed in the 1920s.

metadata.title: Tickets To Travel Ep  10  Beyond the Ticket  Merging Travel with VIP Event Experiences   A Conversa
metadata.author: Tickets To Travel Podcast
metadata.shortDescription: In Episode 10 of Tickets to Travel, we dive into the dynamic world of ticket reselling and hospitality with Jon Allen, co-founder of TKT, the leading provider for UK and European live events paired with exclusive travel packages. From his early days hustling tickets at school to shaping the industry through technology, John shares the journey that led him to redefine event travel. Discover the growing demand for combining travel with unforgettable VIP event experiences and hear firsthand how TKT brings together premium seats, luxury accommodations, and personalized service for fans worldwide. Don't miss this inside look at the evolving ticketing landscape and the future of travel-centered event experiences!

metadata.title: The Hidden System Behind Concert Ticket And Hotel Fees
metadata.author: Consumer Context
metadata.shortDescription:
If a ticket seller adds a 3% card surcharge with no fee-free way to pay online, FTC guidance says it belongs in the ticket price. So which fees can show up late?

Since May 12, 2025, the FTC's Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees has required businesses that advertise prices for live-event tickets and short-term lodging to show the total price upfront. We walk through FTC examples: towel fees, auto-added resort fees, pre-checked boxes and vague fee labels.

You'll see which charges can appear later, what resale ticket sites must disclose, and why a one-month CPI lodging change (about -0.3%, Aug to Sep 2026) can't show the rule's effect.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The 3% Surcharge That Belongs In Price
0:54 What The FTC Fee Rule Covers
1:47 Towel Fees And Pre-Checked Boxes
2:41 Why A Waivable Resort Fee Is Mandatory
3:30 What Can Be Left Out Of The Price
4:37 Vague Fee Labels And Padded Taxes
5:21 Resale Sites And Phantom Tickets
6:11 What Lodging CPI Can And Cannot Show
6:56 Which Fees Were Part Of The Price

KEY TAKEAWAYS
- Since May 12, 2025, ticket and lodging ads with prices must show the total price upfront
- An unavoidable 3% card surcharge belongs in the ticket price, per FTC guidance
- A resort fee waived only if you object is still mandatory under FTC guidance
- Only government charges, shipping and optional extras you choose can be left out upfront
- Vague labels like "service fee" are out, and fee descriptions must be true

#HiddenFees #FTC #ResortFees #ConsumerEconomics

Educational information, not personalized financial advice.


Sources:
CPI-U lodging away from home, US city average, not seasonally adjusted: https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v2/timeseries/data/CUUR0000SEHB
The Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees: Frequently Asked Questions | Federal Trade Commission: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/rule-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-frequently-asked-questions

More The Hidden System episodes: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLWe-dCgqVOzo
keywords: Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees

segments.text: If an online ticket seller adds a 3% credit card surcharge and gives you
no fee-free way to pay online, the FTC's guidance says that 3% belongs
in the ticket price. Not in the fine print.
Not on the last screen.
In the price. That sounds obvious.
But think about how often the number you clicked wasn't the number you paid.
Concert tickets. Hotel rooms. Same story, different checkout page.
Here's what we'll figure out: which fees are actually allowed to show up late,
and which ones were part of the price all along?
Start with the rulebook. Since May 12, 2025, the FTC's Rule
on Unfair or Deceptive Fees has covered two kinds of purchases: live-event tickets
and short-term lodging. That second one is broad.
It covers hotels, motels, inns, short-term rentals and vacation rentals.
The rule bans bait-and-switch pricing and other tactics that hide or misrepresent
the real total. The main requirement is simple.
If a business shows you a price in an ad or an offer, it
has to tell you the total price upfront.
That total includes every fee the business knows about and can calculate in advance.
So the headline number is supposed to be the real number.
But which fees count as fees you have to pay?
The FTC's guidance lists conditions.
One covers anything you must buy to make the thing usable, if a reasonable
person would expect it to be included.
The guidance's example is almost funny.
If a hotel makes guests pay for towels, the towel fee goes in the
total. Another covers fees you can't really agree to.
Think default billing, pre-checked boxes, or opt-out setups.
Ticket fees get the same treatment.
If an online retailer charges a fee to buy tickets online and you can't
avoid it, the guidance says that fee belongs in the total.
Nobody books a room hoping to drip-dry.
Now here's the twist. Picture checking in.
The hotel automatically adds a resort fee for using its facilities.
If you notice and push back, it waives the fee.
So it's optional, right? The FTC's guidance says no.
It calls that resort fee mandatory, for two reasons.
First, you'd reasonably expect to use the facilities as part of your stay.
Second, charging the fee automatically limits your ability to say yes or no.
My read: the trick was never really the fee itself.
It was the default. A charge you have to catch and fight isn't a
choice. It's a toll with a complaint window.
So what can a business leave out of the upfront price?
Only three categories. Government charges.
Shipping charges. And optional extras you choose to add.
The FTC's example is a live music venue selling tickets for $150
and a VIP package for $200 with drinks and an appetizer.
That VIP package is optional, so it doesn't have to be included in the
ticket price. The same goes for hotel trip protection, but only if you check
the box yourself. A pre-checked box is a different story.
Hotels can advertise their lowest available total price, as long as you can
actually book that room at that price.
If you pick an upgrade, the total has to update.
Some charges that come after the purchase can also stay out, like late payment
fees or charges for damaging a room.
And anything left out still has to be clearly shown before you're asked to
pay.
Then there's the wording on the receipt.
Under the rule, businesses have to say what a fee is actually for.
Vague labels like "convenience fee," "service fee" or "processing fee" are out.
The explanation also has to be true.
The FTC's guidance flags a hotel that charges an "environmental fee" but doesn't
use it for sustainability or conservation.
It also flags a resale ticket seller whose "taxes and fees" line pads the
real government taxes and fees with money the seller keeps as profit.
Itemizing is still allowed, so you can see the pieces.
But the total has to be clear and more prominent than anything else.
Concert tickets add another layer: the resale market.
The rule covers it too.
Online marketplaces and other middlemen, including resale ticket sites, have to
give sellers what they need to calculate the total price.
If a platform charges a fee and the seller passes it on to you,
the platform has to tell the seller exactly what that fee is.
In turn, sellers have to give the marketplace accurate prices, fees
included. And a price for tickets that don't exist doesn't count.
The FTC's example is a speculative seller advertising seats to a sold-out concert
that it doesn't actually have.
Those tickets aren't "available," whatever the listing says.
What about the room rate itself?
The government's price survey for lodging away from home, which uses the U.S.
city average and isn't seasonally adjusted, shows a change of about -0.3%
from August to September 2026.
On its own, that one-month move can't tell you whether the rule changed what
you pay. Here's the clever part, though.
All the FTC guidance we've covered is about how prices are shown and described.
It's about making sure the price you compare is the price you pay.
Whether a room is a good deal is still your call.
Now you get to make that call with the real number.
So, back to the question.
Under the FTC's rule, effective May 12, 2025, the only
charges that can show up late are government charges, shipping, optional
extras you choose, and certain charges that come after the purchase.
Any other mandatory fee a business knows about upfront, from a resort fee to
the unavoidable surcharge in the FTC's 3% example, was part of the price all
along. If this helps you read your next
receipt, hit like and subscribe.

So, if we go for smaller venues or venues that, you know, have less remaining tickets relative to the total inventory, maybe GA venues, that's going to really help us narrow down again on exactly what events we want to target. Um if we're looking at these giant stadiums, you know, the the tickets that are going to be remaining is platinum tickets or VIP packages uh packages. We really want to be buying standard tickets, and we don't want to go after stuff that everyone else is already familiar with because you're just going to be dealing with leftover tickets and a lot of competition in terms of what do I want to resell? The goal with this method is again to find events that are unknown, not known about, not targeted by other resellers, but there's still, you know, fans that are interested in this niche artist that have a lot of demand, that has the potential to make 25, 50, 100% profit margin, and those are the events you want to add to your short list. Those are the events you want to monitor and decide, "Hey, do I want to go ahead and jump into this event now and buy some tickets for these events?" Now, one of the strongest signals that we have is when an event shows up in both of these lists. So, there's low remaining inventory, and they're also moving a lot of tickets at the same time. Now, you can wait until the, you know, last day essentially, give it 2, 3 more days, and then buy those tickets, but that is really the best time to buy those tickets because we know that it is essentially on its way to selling out. So, this is the buy section. That's really what we want to recommend you look after. And of course, you want to also make sure that the event still has a enough time to the event. You know, if an event is almost sold out, it's going to sell out in 2, 3 days, but the event is also in 2, 3 days, you don't have any time to actually get in there, buy them, and list them for sale because, you know, they have to go up on StubHub, they have to go on the secondary, and you have to list those tickets. You probably saw in one of those charts that there are areas where the tickets go from 500 down up to 700, and then it continues to sell normally. So, Ticketmaster will hold back or withhold inventory and release more after the presale, after the onsale, they'll randomly release additional tickets. So, sometimes they'll release an additional four-pack or an additional 20, sometimes they'll release an additional 200 seats. You don't know, so you want to keep in mind are they dropping tickets for this event? If you see that trend line or that graph go up and down, that venue is likely to release more tickets down the road. Usually most venues will have you know, only a couple big drops. So, if they have, you know, two to three large drops, you can kind of compare that against the venue capacity. So, we can see what is the total amount of tickets this event can even hold. That way it lets us know, "Hey, there's a chance that they drop tickets or they don't." Um the next one is there were never many tickets moving for this event as at all. So, if there's few tickets remaining, but it's a small venue and it's not moving very well, it's kind [snorts] of just a dud. Sometimes we'll see that with uh small events where there's just not enough demand, there's really no demand on the secondary, it's just kind of one of those small events. The next point to look at is dynamic pricing. So, what that means is Ticketmaster AXS, they'll price their tickets based on the secondary market. metadata.title: Why Are Concert Tickets So Expensive? The Fees After Face Value
metadata.author: Business Made Simple
metadata.shortDescription:
Why are concert tickets so expensive by the time you reach checkout? In this documentary-style explainer, we follow one concert ticket from its listed price all the way to the final total and explain each step in plain English.You'll learn:• The difference between face value and the final price you pay• What ticket service fees are and what they are generally meant to cover• How venue costs and facility charges can be added to a ticket• How dynamic, demand-based ticket pricing works and why prices can change while you browse• What drip pricing means, and how all-in pricing shows the full cost up front• How ticketing businesses make money, explained simplyWhenever we mention a figure, we state the year it applies to and clearly label any estimates, so you know exactly what you're looking at. This video is about understanding how pricing works. It is not about blaming any company or artist.This explainer is made for curious adults, students, freelancers and small-business owners who want to understand why things cost what they cost. The pricing ideas here also apply to many other everyday purchases.If you enjoy plain-English business explainers, subscribe for more videos on how everyday businesses make money.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro
0:22 What does a ticket total look like
1:37 What is face value on a ticket
2:47 What is a ticket service fee
4:12 What are facility and processing charges
5:33 How one fan saw the price change
6:53 What is dynamic ticket pricing
8:11 Why do resale tickets cost even more
